alphabet.bigIdea: Spanish uses many familiar letters, but their names and sounds do not always match English. Learn the alphabet as a way to decode words and spell names—not as a promise that every letter has just one sound.
alphabet.goal: Recognize ñ as a separate letter and distinguish a letter’s name from its sound.

build.title: Start with 27 letters
build.body: The Spanish alphabet has 27 letters. Ñ comes after n and is a separate letter, not an accented version of n. The sequences ch and ll represent sounds but are not separate alphabet letters.

build.title: Separate names from sounds
build.body: The letter h is called hache, but it is normally silent in words such as hola. A letter’s name helps you spell; its sound helps you read.

build.title: Read small groups, not isolated symbols
build.body: Some spellings work together: qu before e or i represents a k sound, as in queso. Learn these combinations alongside whole words.

build.title: Read ll and ch as sound spellings
build.body: Ll in llave and ch in chico each represent a consonant sound. In most Spanish varieties, ll shares its consonant pronunciation with y; regional variants exist. Neither is an extra alphabet letter, but both need a pronunciation rule. See Read Spanish Letter Combinations for ll/y, ch, c/qu, g/j, gue/gui/gü, silent h and b/v.

extraExamples.explanation: The h in hola is silent; begin with the vowel sound.
In quiero and queso, qu represents a k sound and the u is silent.

contrast.title: One letter can change the word

items.explanation: Campana contains n; compare it with campaña, which contains ñ.
Changing n to ñ creates a different word with a different consonant sound.

closerLook.title: Letters vary by region
closerLook.body: Z and c before e/i are commonly pronounced like s in Latin America and parts of Spain. Much of Spain distinguishes them with a sound like th in English thin. Both patterns are standard.

closerLook.title: Spelling your name
closerLook.body: Use letter names when spelling aloud. For example, Ana is a–ene–a. Letter names are vocabulary worth learning separately from pronunciation.

closerLook.title: Start with story words
closerLook.body: Llave, llama, llega and llueve already occur in beginner stories. Read ll together rather than as two English l sounds. Much of Argentina and Uruguay has a sh-like or zh-like ll/y; many other regions use a y-like sound, and some distinguish ll from y.

mistakes.incorrect: hola with an English h sound
mistakes.explanation: The written h usually does not represent a spoken consonant.

mistakes.correct: Treat ñ as a separate letter
mistakes.explanation: The tongue movement and word meaning can change.

practice.prompt: Which letter comes after n?
practice.explanation: Ñ has its own place in the 27-letter alphabet.

practice.prompt: Does the h in hola sound like English h?
practice.explanation: The letter name hache does not tell you to pronounce h inside the word.

practice.prompt: In queso, do you pronounce the u separately?
practice.explanation: Qu before e forms the spelling for a k sound.

takeaways: Learn letter names for spelling and sound patterns for reading.
Ñ and n are different letters.
Learn combinations such as qu in whole words.
Alphabet classification is not a substitute for spelling-to-sound rules such as ll and ch.

vowels.bigIdea: Spanish has five basic vowel sounds. Compared with English, they are relatively steady: an unstressed vowel usually stays recognizable instead of fading into an “uh” sound.
vowels.goal: Keep vowels clear in both stressed and unstressed syllables.

build.title: Give each vowel a target
build.body: A is an open ah sound; e is a pure mid-front sound; i resembles ee; o is a pure rounded sound; u resembles oo. English comparisons are starting points, not exact matches.

build.title: Keep the sound steady
build.body: Avoid adding a glide to e or o. Say no with one steady o rather than the changing vowel often heard in English no.

build.title: Keep unstressed vowels alive
build.body: In casa, both a vowels remain clear even though the first syllable is stressed. Less stress does not mean replacing the vowel with uh.

extraExamples.explanation: Keep the o vowels in no and tomo steady; café ends with a stressed e.
The u in tu and the i in libro are clear vowels; aquí ends with a stressed i.

contrast.title: Stress changes emphasis, not the vowel’s identity

items.explanation: The final a is unstressed but stays an a.
The stressed e gets emphasis without becoming an English ay glide.

closerLook.title: Two vowels can share a syllable
closerLook.body: In words such as aire or ciudad, vowels can form a diphthong. In other words they form separate syllables. Learn syllable patterns after establishing the five basic sounds.

closerLook.title: Silent u is a spelling exception
closerLook.body: The u is normally silent in que, qui, gue and gui. A diaeresis makes it sound in güe/güi, as in pingüino.

mistakes.incorrect: casa ending in an English uh sound
mistakes.correct: casa with a clear final a
mistakes.explanation: Unstressed Spanish vowels usually retain their quality.

mistakes.incorrect: no with an exaggerated oh-oo glide
mistakes.explanation: A pure vowel helps keep Spanish rhythm clear.

practice.prompt: Which vowel should stay clear at the end of casa?
practice.explanation: It is unstressed, but it does not normally become a neutral uh.

practice.prompt: How many basic vowel sounds are the starting point?
practice.answer: Five: a, e, i, o, u.
practice.explanation: Spellings and combinations add detail, but these are the foundation.

practice.prompt: Should the e in café turn into ay?
practice.explanation: Stress makes it prominent, not a different vowel.

takeaways: Keep a, e, i, o and u distinct.
Avoid English-style vowel glides and reductions.
Check special spellings before assuming every written vowel sounds.

stress.bigIdea: Every ordinary multi-syllable word has a stressed syllable: its most prominent beat. Spanish spelling often tells you where that beat belongs. Spoken stress is present whether or not an accent is written.
stress.goal: Use the default stress patterns and written accents to find the prominent syllable.

build.title: Check for an accent first
build.body: First separate the word into syllables: casa → ca-sa; teléfono → te-lé-fo-no. A written acute accent identifies the stressed vowel: café is ca-FÉ and teléfono is te-LÉ-fo-no. If vowel combinations make the syllables unclear, use the vowel-combinations lesson first.

build.title: Look at the ending
build.body: Without an accent, words ending in a vowel, n or s normally stress the next-to-last syllable: casa, comen, lunes. Words ending in most other consonants normally stress the last: hotel, hablar.

build.title: Say the whole word
build.body: Keep other syllables clear while giving the stressed syllable more prominence. Stress does not require shouting or swallowing the remaining vowels.

extraExamples.explanation: Hotel ends in l and has no accent: ho-TEL.
The accent overrides the default: te-LÉ-fo-no.

contrast.title: The same letters can carry different stress

items.explanation: Hablo ends in a vowel with no accent: HA-blo.
The accent marks ha-BLÓ; this is a different verb form.

closerLook.title: A useful boundary
closerLook.body: Unusual consonant groups and vowel combinations need additional rules. Start with ordinary words and consult pronunciation when syllable division is uncertain.

closerLook.title: Stress can move in your attention, not in the word
closerLook.body: Emphasizing a whole word in a sentence does not move its lexical stress to another syllable.

closerLook.title: Word stress versus sentence emphasis
closerLook.body: You may emphasize yo in Yo hablo, but hablo remains HA-blo. Moving stress to ha-BLÓ changes the verb to a past form. Sentence focus does not create a new written accent.

mistakes.explanation: The default for a word ending in l is final-syllable stress.
The accent explicitly identifies the stressed vowel.

practice.prompt: Where is the stress in casa?
practice.explanation: It ends in a vowel and has no accent.

practice.prompt: Where is the stress in hablar?
practice.explanation: It ends in r, so the usual default is final stress.

practice.prompt: What changes between hablo and habló?
practice.explanation: HA-blo means I speak; ha-BLÓ means he/she/you formal spoke.

takeaways: Check written accents first.
Vowel, n or s usually means next-to-last stress.
Most other consonant endings usually mean final stress.

rr.bigIdea: Spanish distinguishes a quick tap from a trill. In the middle of a word, this difference can change the meaning, so practice it as a sound contrast rather than a louder English r.
rr.goal: Recognize where the tap and trill occur and compare a minimal pair.

build.title: Make a quick tap
build.body: For the r in caro, the tongue tip briefly taps the ridge just behind your upper teeth. The American English middle sound in butter can be a rough starting point.

build.title: Let the tongue vibrate
build.body: For rr in carro, airflow helps a relaxed tongue tip vibrate near that ridge. Extra throat tension usually makes it harder.

build.title: Read the position
build.body: Between vowels, r usually signals the tap and rr the trill. A word-initial r also uses the strong sound: rojo. You never need rr at the start of an ordinary word.

extraExamples.explanation: Caro has a single r between vowels: use a tap.
Carro has rr, while rojo begins with r; both use the strong r sound.

contrast.title: One extra r, a different word

items.explanation: Caro uses the tap.
Carro uses the trill. Carro is a common word for car in many regions.

closerLook.title: Other strong-r positions
closerLook.body: R is also strong after n, l and s, as in enredo or alrededor. Consonant clusters such as pr in primo generally use a tap.

closerLook.title: Progress before perfection
closerLook.body: If the trill is not available yet, keep practicing short relaxed attempts. Understanding the contrast is useful before you can produce it consistently.

mistakes.incorrect: rr pronounced as an English throat r
mistakes.correct: rr made near the ridge behind the teeth
mistakes.explanation: The Spanish sound depends on the tongue tip and airflow.
Initial r already represents the strong sound.

practice.prompt: Which has the tap: caro or carro?
practice.explanation: A single r between vowels normally represents the tap.

practice.prompt: Does rojo need rr at the start?
practice.explanation: Initial r already takes the strong pronunciation.

practice.prompt: Where should the tongue tip work?
practice.answer: Near the ridge behind the upper teeth.
practice.explanation: Avoid trying to force the sound from the throat.

takeaways: Between vowels, r and rr distinguish sounds.
Initial r uses the strong sound.
Practice relaxed tongue-tip movement rather than force.

gender.bigIdea: Spanish nouns belong to grammatical gender classes. Gender helps nearby words fit together; it does not mean that objects have a biological sex.
gender.goal: Learn nouns with their articles and carry agreement into descriptions.

build.title: Learn the noun with el or la
build.body: Store el libro and la mesa as small units. The article gives you gender information that a bare noun may not reveal.

build.title: Use endings as clues
build.body: Many nouns in -o are masculine and many in -a are feminine. These are patterns, not guarantees: el día and la mano are common exceptions.

build.title: Carry gender into agreement
build.body: A describing word often changes: el libro nuevo, la mesa nueva. Some adjectives, such as interesante, use the same form for either gender.

extraExamples.explanation: Mano is feminine despite ending in -o; fría agrees with it.
Día is masculine despite ending in -a; largo agrees with it.

items.explanation: Libro is masculine, so use el and nuevo.
Mesa is feminine, so use la and nueva.

closerLook.title: People and grammatical gender
closerLook.body: Some nouns for people vary by article: el estudiante / la estudiante. Others have different endings. Learn the whole expression rather than changing every noun mechanically.

closerLook.title: El agua is still feminine
closerLook.body: A stressed initial a sound can trigger el with a singular feminine noun: el agua fría. The adjective remains feminine; the plural is las aguas.

mistakes.explanation: The -a ending is not a guarantee of feminine gender.
The adjective agrees with the noun, not with the speaker.

practice.prompt: Choose: el or la mano.
practice.explanation: Mano is a common feminine noun ending in -o.

practice.prompt: Complete: la casa blanc__.
practice.explanation: Casa is feminine singular, so blanca matches it.

practice.prompt: Is agua masculine because we say el agua?
practice.explanation: The singular article changes before stressed initial a; agreement stays feminine.

takeaways: Learn nouns together with their articles.
Endings are clues, with exceptions.
Gender agreement follows the noun.

articles.bigIdea: Articles help a listener tell whether you mean an identifiable thing or are introducing one. Spanish also uses articles in places where English may leave them out.
articles.goal: Choose definite and indefinite articles and match gender and number.

build.title: Choose identifiable or newly introduced
build.body: El/la often point to something identifiable in context. Un/una often introduce one member of a group: un libro, then el libro.

build.title: Match the noun
build.body: Definite articles are el, la, los, las. Indefinite articles are un, una, unos, unas. Select both gender and number: unas mesas.

build.title: Notice Spanish habits
build.body: Spanish often uses a definite article to speak about a category: Me gusta el café. An English translation may simply say I like coffee.

extraExamples.spanish: Compré un libro. El libro es corto.
extraExamples.english: I bought a book. The book is short.
extraExamples.explanation: Un introduces the book; el refers back to the now-identifiable book.
Ventanas is feminine plural, so use las.

items.explanation: Una introduces a pharmacy.

items.spanish: La farmacia cierra a las ocho.
items.explanation: La can identify the pharmacy already under discussion.

closerLook.title: Not every noun needs an article
closerLook.body: After ser, an unmodified profession often has no article: Soy profesora. Modifying or evaluating it can change the pattern: Es una profesora excelente.

closerLook.title: Two contractions
closerLook.body: A + el becomes al and de + el becomes del: Voy al parque; Vengo del trabajo. This does not happen with la, los or las.

mistakes.explanation: Libros is masculine plural.
A and the article el contract to al.

practice.prompt: Introduce a feminine singular house: __ casa.
practice.explanation: Una introduces one house and matches its gender.

practice.prompt: Refer back to those books: __ libros.
practice.explanation: The definite masculine plural article is los.

practice.prompt: Combine de + el mercado.
practice.explanation: De and the article el contract to del.

takeaways: Use context to choose identifiable or newly introduced.
Match article gender and number.
Learn article usage through Spanish patterns, not just English translations.

plural.bigIdea: When a noun becomes plural, the words describing or introducing it often change too. Think of number as an agreement chain rather than one extra s.
plural.goal: Form common plurals and update articles and adjectives alongside them.

build.title: Choose the noun ending
build.body: Most nouns ending in an unstressed vowel add -s: casa → casas. Many ending in a consonant add -es: papel → papeles.

build.title: Handle z and accents
build.body: Final z changes to c before -es: luz → luces. Accent marks may change to preserve the stress pattern: canción → canciones.

build.title: Update the whole group
build.body: La casa blanca becomes las casas blancas. The article, noun and adjective all signal plural.

extraExamples.explanation: Las, casas and blancas all show plural agreement.
Luz becomes luces: z changes to c before -es.

items.explanation: Each word is singular.
El becomes los; papel and azul add -es.

closerLook.title: Some nouns keep their form
closerLook.body: Words such as lunes and paraguas can have the same singular and plural form: el lunes / los lunes. The article helps identify number.

closerLook.title: Not all vowel endings behave alike
closerLook.body: Stressed -í and -ú have additional patterns and variants. Treat the basic -s/-es rules as a starting point and check unfamiliar forms.

mistakes.explanation: The noun and adjective must agree with the plural article.
Final z changes to c before -es.

practice.prompt: Make el libro rojo plural.
practice.explanation: All three words change to plural.

practice.prompt: Make la luz plural.
practice.explanation: Change the article and replace z with c before -es.

practice.prompt: Why does canción lose its accent in canciones?
practice.answer: The default stress rule now puts stress in the right place.
practice.explanation: Canciones ends in s and naturally stresses the next-to-last syllable.

takeaways: Form the noun plural, then check nearby agreement.
Final z becomes c before -es.
Preserve stress even when the accent spelling changes.

adjectives.bigIdea: Adjectives describe nouns. Many Spanish adjectives adjust their endings to match the noun, and their position can affect how a description feels or what it means.
adjectives.goal: Match common adjective endings and use a dependable default word order.

build.title: Match gender when the form changes
build.body: Adjectives ending in -o often change to -a with feminine nouns: un libro rojo, una casa roja. Adjectives such as grande and interesante do not change for gender.

build.title: Match number too
build.body: Add the appropriate plural ending: libros rojos, casas grandes. Even adjectives with one gender form normally change for number.

build.title: Start after the noun
build.body: For a neutral description, noun + adjective is a useful starting point: una mesa pequeña. Position is flexible, but not every position has the same meaning.

extraExamples.explanation: Pequeñas agrees with the feminine plural subject casas.
Interesante has one gender form but adds -s for plural.

items.explanation: Rojo matches masculine singular coche.
Rojas matches feminine plural casas.

closerLook.title: Position can change meaning
closerLook.body: Un amigo viejo is an elderly friend; un viejo amigo is a longstanding friend. Learn these contrasts as phrases rather than moving adjectives freely.

closerLook.title: Some forms shorten before a noun
closerLook.body: Bueno becomes buen before a masculine singular noun: un buen libro. Grande often becomes gran before a singular noun: una gran idea.

mistakes.explanation: Roja agrees with casa, regardless of who owns it.
The adjective must match plural number.

practice.prompt: Complete: las mesas pequeñ__.
practice.explanation: Feminine plural requires -as.

practice.prompt: Describe two interesting books.
practice.explanation: Interesante does not change gender, but it does change number.

practice.prompt: Does un viejo amigo necessarily mean an elderly friend?
practice.answer: No; it usually means a longstanding friend.
practice.explanation: Adjective position can change the interpretation.

takeaways: Check the noun’s gender and number.
Not every adjective has separate masculine and feminine forms.
After the noun is a useful default, not an absolute rule.

comparisons.bigIdea: Comparisons place two things on a shared scale. Spanish uses different patterns for more/less and for equality, so first decide what relationship you want to express.
comparisons.goal: Compare qualities and quantities using más, menos, tan and tanto.

build.title: Compare a quality
build.body: Use más/menos + adjective + que: Ana es más alta que Luis. The adjective still agrees with the thing being described.

build.title: Express equal quality
build.body: Use tan + adjective + como: La casa es tan grande como el piso. Tan does not change its ending.

build.title: Compare amounts
build.body: Use más/menos + noun + que. For equal amounts use tanto/tanta/tantos/tantas + noun + como: Tengo tantos libros como tú. Tanto matches the noun.

extraExamples.spanish: Este libro es menos caro que ese.
extraExamples.english: This book is less expensive than that one.
extraExamples.explanation: Menos + adjective + que compares the price.

extraExamples.english: I have as many questions as you.
extraExamples.explanation: Tantas agrees with feminine plural preguntas.

items.spanish: Es tan interesante como el otro.
items.english: It is as interesting as the other one.
items.explanation: Tan modifies the adjective interesante.

items.spanish: Tiene tantos capítulos como el otro.
items.english: It has as many chapters as the other one.
items.explanation: Tantos modifies masculine plural capítulos.

closerLook.title: Irregular comparisons
closerLook.body: Bueno often becomes mejor and malo becomes peor: Este libro es mejor. Do not add más to mejor or peor in these ordinary comparisons.

closerLook.title: An amount above a number
closerLook.body: Use más de before a numerical threshold: más de diez libros. This differs from comparing two things with más…que.

mistakes.explanation: Mejor already means better.
A noun needs the quantity form tantos, not tan.

practice.prompt: Say: Ana is taller than Luis.
practice.answer: Ana es más alta que Luis.
practice.explanation: Use más + adjective + que; alta agrees with Ana.

practice.prompt: Complete: Tengo __ tiempo como tú.
practice.explanation: Tiempo is masculine singular, so use tanto.

practice.prompt: Say: more than ten books.
practice.explanation: A numerical threshold uses de.

takeaways: Más/menos…que compare differences.
Tan…como compares qualities; tanto…como compares amounts.
Mejor and peor already express a comparison.

subject-pronouns.bigIdea: A subject pronoun names who does something: I, you, we. Spanish verb endings often carry that information already, so pronouns are useful choices rather than mandatory sentence starters.
subject-pronouns.goal: Identify subjects and decide when a pronoun adds useful information.

build.title: Know the main forms
build.body: Yo means I; tú means informal singular you; él/ella mean he/she; usted is formal singular you; nosotros/nosotras mean we; ellos/ellas mean they; ustedes means plural you.

build.title: Let the ending do its work
build.body: Hablo español is a complete sentence. Hablo identifies yo, so adding yo is optional unless you want emphasis or contrast.

build.title: Use a pronoun to clarify or contrast
build.body: Él habla and ella habla have the same verb ending. A pronoun or name can clarify who you mean. Yo estudio, pero él trabaja creates a contrast.

extraExamples.explanation: The -amos ending identifies nosotros/nosotras without an explicit pronoun.
The pronouns highlight a contrast between who does each task.

contrast.title: The pronoun adds emphasis, not a new action

items.explanation: A neutral statement; the verb identifies the speaker.
Yo can emphasize or contrast the speaker, depending on context.

closerLook.title: Plural you varies by region
closerLook.body: In most of Spain, vosotros/vosotras is informal plural you. Ustedes is the usual plural you throughout Latin America and also occurs in parts of Spain.

closerLook.title: Usted uses third-person grammar
closerLook.body: Although usted addresses the listener, it takes habla, not hablas. Ustedes takes hablan.

mistakes.explanation: The verb ending must match yo.
Usted takes the third-person singular form.

practice.prompt: Who is implied by hablamos?
practice.explanation: The -amos ending identifies we.

practice.prompt: Must you put yo before hablo?
practice.explanation: The ending already identifies the subject; yo can add emphasis.

practice.prompt: Complete: usted __ español. (hablar)
practice.explanation: Formal you uses the third-person singular form.

takeaways: Match the verb to the subject.
Omit a pronoun when the subject is clear.
Include it for clarity, emphasis or contrast.

tu-usted.bigIdea: Spanish has more than one way to address one person. Tú and usted both mean you, but they signal different relationships and require different verb forms.
tu-usted.goal: Keep your chosen form of address consistent across verbs and possessives.

build.title: Choose the relationship
build.body: Tú is often used with friends, family and peers. Usted can express respect or distance. Age, region, workplace and personal preference all affect the choice.

build.title: Match the verb pattern
build.body: Tú hablas, comes, vives; usted habla, come, vive. Usted shares its verb forms with él and ella even though you are speaking to the listener.

build.title: Keep nearby words consistent
build.body: With tú, use your forms such as tu casa. With usted, use su casa. Subject tú has an accent; possessive tu does not.

extraExamples.explanation: Trabajas matches tú. The pronoun can be omitted.
Trabaja matches usted and can also appear without the pronoun when context is clear.

items.explanation: Estás addresses tú.
Está addresses usted; the pronoun makes the intended subject explicit.

closerLook.title: No universal stranger rule
closerLook.body: Some communities use tú readily with strangers; others prefer usted more often. Listen to local usage and follow the other person’s preference.

closerLook.title: Another form: vos
closerLook.body: Many regions use vos with its own patterns, such as vos hablás. Recognize this as a legitimate regional system, not a mistake.

mistakes.explanation: Usted takes the third-person singular verb form.
The subject pronoun tú has an accent; possessive tu does not.

practice.prompt: Make ¿Cómo estás? formal.
practice.explanation: Change estás to está; usted can clarify the addressee.

practice.prompt: Complete: tú __ aquí. (vivir)
practice.explanation: The tú form ends in -es.

practice.prompt: Is usted always required with every stranger?
practice.explanation: The appropriate choice depends on region, situation and preference.

takeaways: Tú and usted both address one person.
The choice changes the verb pattern.
Use local context rather than a rigid age rule.

possessives.bigIdea: Possessive words show a relationship such as my book or our house. Their endings usually match the thing possessed—not the gender of the owner.
possessives.goal: Choose a possessive for the owner and match it to the noun.

build.title: Choose the owner
build.body: Before a noun, use mi for my, tu for your informal singular, su for his/her/your formal/their, and nuestro/nuestra for our.

build.title: Match the number of things
build.body: Mi libro becomes mis libros. Tu casa becomes tus casas. Mi, tu and su change for number but not gender.

build.title: Match nuestro for both features
build.body: Nuestro libro, nuestra casa, nuestros libros, nuestras casas. The ending follows the possessed noun.

build.title: Use the full form when the noun is understood
build.body: Es mía means it is mine, referring to a feminine singular noun such as llave. El libro es mío and las llaves son mías follow the possessed noun’s gender and number. Full forms include mío/tuyo/suyo and their feminine/plural forms; nuestro already has full-form endings.

extraExamples.explanation: Mi is singular with hermano; mis is plural with llaves. The owner is the same.
Nuestra agrees with feminine singular casa.
Mía agrees with an understood feminine noun such as llave, not the owner’s gender.

items.explanation: Su agrees with one book and does not reveal the owner’s identity.
Sus agrees with plural keys; it does not mean there are multiple owners.

closerLook.title: Clarify su when needed
closerLook.body: Su casa can be ambiguous. La casa de Ana or la casa de ustedes makes the owner explicit.

closerLook.title: Possessives after the noun
closerLook.body: Un amigo mío and la casa es mía use another set of forms. Learn those separately rather than placing mi after a noun.

mistakes.explanation: The possessive matches the plural noun.
Nuestro changes gender as well as number.

practice.prompt: Say: my houses.
practice.explanation: Plural casas requires mis.

practice.prompt: Say: our books.
practice.explanation: Libros is masculine plural.

practice.prompt: Does sus libros tell you there are several owners?
practice.explanation: Sus marks multiple books; the owner needs context.

takeaways: Choose by owner; adjust by the thing owned.
Mi, tu and su change only for number.
Nuestro changes for gender and number.

object-pronouns.bigIdea: A direct object receives the action of a verb. Instead of repeating a known thing, Spanish can replace it with lo, la, los or las.
object-pronouns.goal: Find the direct object and place its replacement before a conjugated verb.

build.title: Find what receives the action
build.body: In Leo el libro, ask “I read what?” El libro is the direct object. The subject yo is the person reading.

build.title: Choose the matching pronoun
build.body: Use lo for masculine singular, la for feminine singular, los for masculine plural and las for feminine plural: la carta → la.

build.title: Put it before the conjugated verb
build.body: Leo el libro becomes Lo leo. The pronoun usually comes before a simple conjugated verb, unlike English I read it.

build.title: People can be direct objects too
build.body: Me, te, nos and os can represent people as direct objects: Te espero means I am waiting for you; Nos ve means he/she sees us. With le/les, check whether the person is a recipient or experiencer. Me and te alone do not tell you whether their role is direct or indirect; the verb pattern does.

extraExamples.spanish: Compro las entradas. Las compro hoy.
extraExamples.english: I buy the tickets. I buy them today.
extraExamples.explanation: Las replaces feminine plural entradas and goes before compro.

extraExamples.english: Do you have the book? Yes, I have it.
extraExamples.explanation: Lo replaces masculine singular libro; tengo still agrees with yo.

extraExamples.english: I am waiting for you at the café.
extraExamples.explanation: Te is the direct object of esperar here, not a recipient of a thing.

contrast.title: The noun changes; the subject does not

items.english: I read the letter. I read it.
items.explanation: La replaces the feminine singular object.

items.english: I read the messages. I read them.
items.explanation: Los replaces the masculine plural object.

closerLook.title: Two places with an infinitive
closerLook.body: Lo voy a leer and Voy a leerlo both work. Put the pronoun before the conjugated verb or attach it to the infinitive; do not put it between a and leer.

closerLook.title: Direct versus indirect objects
closerLook.body: In Le doy el libro a Ana, le marks the recipient, not the book. Regional leísmo adds further variation; this lesson starts with the standard thing-replacement pattern.

closerLook.title: Compare the same pronoun in two roles
closerLook.body: Te veo uses te as the person seen, a direct object. Te doy agua uses te as the recipient, an indirect object; agua is the thing given. The familiar English translation is not enough to identify the grammatical role.

mistakes.explanation: Before a simple conjugated verb, put the pronoun first.

mistakes.incorrect: La leo. when replacing el libro
mistakes.explanation: Match the object’s grammatical gender, not the reader’s gender.

practice.prompt: Replace la película in Veo la película.
practice.explanation: La replaces the feminine singular object and precedes veo.

practice.prompt: Replace los libros in Tengo los libros.
practice.explanation: Los is masculine plural.

practice.prompt: Give one version of I am going to read it, referring to el libro.
practice.answer: Lo voy a leer. / Voy a leerlo.
practice.explanation: Both positions are valid with this infinitive construction.

takeaways: Find the object before choosing the pronoun.
Lo/la/los/las match the object.
Place it before a conjugated verb or attach it to an infinitive.

reflexive.bigIdea: In a reflexive action, the person doing something also receives the action. Spanish uses a small pronoun to show this link, though not every verb with se has a literal “self” meaning.
reflexive.goal: Match reflexive pronouns and distinguish an action on yourself from one on someone else.

build.title: Pair the subject and pronoun
build.body: Yo me, tú te, él/ella/usted se, nosotros/nosotras nos, ellos/ellas/ustedes se. With vosotros/vosotras, use os.

build.title: Conjugate the verb too
build.body: Lavarse is the dictionary form. Me lavo means I wash myself; te lavas means you wash yourself. Both the pronoun and verb track the subject.

build.title: Place the pronoun
build.body: Use Me voy a lavar or Voy a lavarme with an infinitive. With a simple conjugated verb, use Me lavo.

extraExamples.explanation: Me and levanto both refer to yo. Levantarse is learned as a complete verb pattern.
Nos refers back to we. Spanish commonly uses the article las with body parts in this pattern.

items.explanation: Someone else receives the washing.
Me links the receiver to the speaker.

closerLook.title: Se does more than reflexive work
closerLook.body: Se vende pan and Se lo doy use se for different reasons. Do not translate every se as himself or herself.

closerLook.title: Meaning can shift
closerLook.body: Ir means go; irse often means leave. Learn the whole expression rather than assuming the pronoun just adds self.

mistakes.explanation: The reflexive pronoun must match yo.
A simple personal statement needs a conjugated verb.

practice.prompt: Say: you wash yourself, using tú.
practice.explanation: Both te and lavas match tú.

practice.prompt: Say: we get up early.
practice.explanation: Use nos and the nosotros verb ending.

practice.prompt: Must se always mean herself or himself?
practice.explanation: Reflexive use is only one of several se patterns.

takeaways: Match both pronoun and verb to the subject.
Use the article with body parts in patterns such as me lavo las manos.
Learn verbs with se as complete expressions.

infinitives.bigIdea: An infinitive is the dictionary form of a verb: hablar, comer, vivir. It names an action without saying who does it or when.
infinitives.goal: Recognize infinitives and use them after common verb and preposition patterns.

build.title: Recognize the three endings
build.body: Spanish infinitives end in -ar, -er or -ir. These endings group verbs into families that share many conjugation patterns.

build.title: Conjugate the verb that carries the sentence
build.body: In Quiero comer, quiero tells you who wants something. Comer names the wanted action and stays in its dictionary form.

build.title: Use infinitives after prepositions
build.body: Para aprender means in order to learn. Antes de salir means before leaving. English may use -ing where Spanish uses an infinitive.

extraExamples.explanation: Necesito is conjugated for yo; estudiar stays in the infinitive.

extraExamples.english: I read in order to learn.
extraExamples.explanation: After para, aprender names the purpose without a personal ending.

contrast.title: Name the action or say who does it

items.explanation: The infinitive phrase acts as the subject.
Hablo is a personal verb form identifying yo.

closerLook.title: Two verbs do not always mean an infinitive
closerLook.body: Quiero estudiar works, but Quiero que estudies uses a clause with its own subject. The relationship between the actions determines the structure.

closerLook.title: Infinitive is not always English to
closerLook.body: Me gusta leer translates as I like reading or I like to read. Translate the whole expression, not a fixed word for word label.

mistakes.explanation: After quiero with the same intended actor, use the infinitive.
The verb directly after this preposition stays in the infinitive.

practice.prompt: Which family does vivir belong to?
practice.explanation: Its dictionary ending identifies the group.

practice.prompt: Complete: Necesito __. (to eat)
practice.explanation: Necesito carries the subject; comer names the action.

practice.prompt: Translate before leaving.
practice.explanation: Use an infinitive after de in this expression.

takeaways: Infinitives end in -ar, -er or -ir.
They name actions without personal endings.
Learn the surrounding pattern to decide whether an infinitive belongs.

present-ar.bigIdea: Regular -ar verbs share a set of present-tense endings. Once you know the pattern, you can apply it to many new verbs while keeping the subject clear.
present-ar.goal: Build present forms of regular -ar verbs and recognize their uses.

build.title: Find the stem
build.body: Remove -ar from hablar to get habl-. Keep this stem for a regular present-tense verb.

build.title: Choose the ending
build.body: Use yo -o, tú -as, él/ella/usted -a, nosotros -amos, vosotros -áis, ellos/ustedes -an: hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan.

build.title: Let context supply the time meaning
build.body: Trabajo can mean I work or I am working. The simple present can express habits, general situations and some current actions.

extraExamples.explanation: Trabaj- + -amos identifies nosotros and describes a habit.
Two named people form a plural subject, so use -an.

items.explanation: Habl- takes -o for yo.
The stem stays; -as identifies tú.

closerLook.title: Not every -ar verb is regular
closerLook.body: Estar and dar have irregular forms. Pensar changes its stem in several persons. Knowing the family helps, but check a new verb’s pattern.

closerLook.title: A shared form across tenses
closerLook.body: Hablamos can mean we speak or we spoke. Context and time expressions distinguish present from preterite.

mistakes.explanation: Yo requires -o in this regular pattern.
Use -amos for nosotros, not the they ending.

practice.prompt: Say: you work, using tú.
practice.explanation: Remove -ar and add -as.

practice.prompt: Say: we study.
practice.explanation: Estudi- + -amos.

practice.prompt: Can hablo mean I am speaking?
practice.explanation: Spanish present tense covers more than English’s simple-present translation.

takeaways: Remove -ar, then add the subject ending.
Use the pattern only for regular verbs.
Context tells you whether the present describes a habit or a current situation.

present-er-ir.bigIdea: Regular -er and -ir verbs use closely related present-tense endings. Learn what they share and notice the two plural forms where the families differ.
present-er-ir.goal: Conjugate regular -er and -ir verbs without mixing their nosotros and vosotros endings.

build.title: Start with the stem
build.body: Comer becomes com-; vivir becomes viv-. Add the ending to this stem.

build.title: Learn the shared endings
build.body: Both families use -o, -es, -e and -en for yo, tú, él/ella/usted and ellos/ustedes: como/vivo, comes/vives, come/vive, comen/viven.

build.title: Keep the plural differences
build.body: Nosotros uses comemos but vivimos. Vosotros uses coméis but vivís. The -er family keeps e; the -ir family uses i in these forms.

extraExamples.explanation: Com- takes -emos for nosotros.
Viv- takes -imos for nosotros.

contrast.title: The family matters in the we form

items.explanation: Beber is an -er verb: -emos.
Abrir is an -ir verb: -imos.

closerLook.title: Regular endings do not guarantee a regular stem
closerLook.body: Pedir and dormir have stem changes; tener has additional irregularities. Learn those as related patterns later.

closerLook.title: Present or past?
closerLook.body: Vivimos can mean we live or we lived. A time phrase and the surrounding story clarify which tense is intended.

mistakes.explanation: An -ir verb uses -imos for nosotros.
The tú ending is -es in both regular families.

practice.prompt: Say: you eat, using tú.
practice.explanation: Com- + -es.

practice.prompt: Say: we open.
practice.explanation: Abrir uses -imos for nosotros.

practice.prompt: Say: they live.
practice.explanation: Both families use -en for ellos/ellas/ustedes.

takeaways: Most present endings are shared by -er and -ir.
Nosotros and vosotros distinguish the families.
Check for irregular stems before applying the regular pattern.

ser-estar.bigIdea: Ser and estar both translate as to be, but they frame information differently. The useful distinction is characterization versus state or location—not permanent versus temporary.
ser-estar.goal: Choose ser or estar by the job it does in the sentence.

build.title: Use ser to identify or characterize
build.body: Soy Ana identifies a person. Es médica gives a profession. El libro es interesante characterizes a book. Ser also handles origin, time and material.

build.title: Use estar for states and locations
build.body: Estoy cansada describes a state. El libro está en la mesa gives an object’s location. A location can be long-lasting and still use estar.

build.title: Watch the adjective’s meaning
build.body: Es aburrido characterizes someone as boring; está aburrido describes someone as bored. The verb can change the interpretation, not just the duration.

extraExamples.explanation: A stable geographic location uses estar, which disproves the temporary-only shortcut.

extraExamples.spanish: La reunión es en la oficina.
extraExamples.english: The meeting is in the office.
extraExamples.explanation: The location of an event commonly uses ser: where it takes place.

items.explanation: Ser presents a characteristic.
Estar presents his state.

closerLook.title: Learn useful forms together
closerLook.body: Ser: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son. Estar: estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están. Both are irregular.

closerLook.title: Event location is a special pattern
closerLook.body: Objects and people are located with estar. Saying where a party, class or meeting takes place commonly uses ser.

mistakes.explanation: Geographic location uses estar even when it is stable.

mistakes.incorrect: La fiesta está en mi casa. for where it takes place
mistakes.correct: La fiesta es en mi casa.
mistakes.explanation: Event location normally uses ser.

practice.prompt: Complete: El libro __ en la mesa.
practice.explanation: You are locating an object.

practice.prompt: Complete: Ana __ médica.
practice.explanation: A profession identifies or characterizes someone.

practice.prompt: Does temporary versus permanent explain every choice?
practice.explanation: Location and event-location patterns show why the shortcut fails.

takeaways: Ask whether you are identifying, characterizing, locating or describing a state.
Duration alone does not choose the verb.
Learn adjective meanings with ser and estar.

hay.bigIdea: Hay introduces the existence or presence of something. Use it to say what is available or what there is; use estar when locating an identifiable thing.
hay.goal: Distinguish introducing something from locating something already identified.

build.title: Introduce what exists
build.body: Hay un banco aquí means there is a bank here. The listener is learning that a bank exists in this place.

build.title: Keep hay with plural nouns
build.body: Hay una mesa and Hay tres mesas use the same form. Do not change hay to match the noun’s number.

build.title: Locate an identified thing with estar
build.body: El banco está aquí locates the bank the listener can identify. Compare an introduction with hay and a location statement with está/están.

extraExamples.spanish: Hay dos ventanas en la habitación.
extraExamples.english: There are two windows in the room.
extraExamples.explanation: Hay stays unchanged with plural ventanas.
The identified windows take están; this describes their state.

items.explanation: Introduce the presence of a pharmacy.
Locate the identified pharmacy.

closerLook.title: Past existence
closerLook.body: The standard impersonal forms also remain singular in the past: había muchas personas; hubo problemas. This is different from ordinary subject-verb agreement.

closerLook.title: A different pattern: hay que
closerLook.body: Hay que estudiar means one must study / studying is necessary. Learn hay que + infinitive as a separate construction.

mistakes.explanation: Hay is unchanged for singular and plural.
Use estar to locate an identified pharmacy.

practice.prompt: Say: there are three books.
practice.explanation: Use hay with plural nouns too.

practice.prompt: Complete: El libro __ aquí.
practice.explanation: You are locating the identified book.

practice.prompt: Say: there is no water.
practice.explanation: Put no before hay.

takeaways: Hay introduces existence or availability.
Hay does not change for plural nouns.
Estar locates identified people and things.

ir-future.bigIdea: Ir + a + infinitive lets you talk about intentions and expected future events. The part that changes is ir; the action you plan stays in its dictionary form.
ir-future.goal: Build future plans for different subjects using ir a.

build.title: Choose the form of ir
build.body: Voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van match yo, tú, él/ella/usted, nosotros, vosotros and ellos/ustedes.

build.title: Keep the connecting a
build.body: Voy a estudiar has three pieces: a form of ir, a, and an infinitive. The a belongs even though English may not suggest a separate word.

build.title: Leave the planned action unconjugated
build.body: Vamos a comer means we are going to eat. Vamos identifies we; comer names the action without another personal ending.

extraExamples.spanish: Vamos a cenar a las ocho.
extraExamples.english: We are going to have dinner at eight.
extraExamples.explanation: Vamos matches we; cenar stays in the infinitive.

extraExamples.english: Ana is going to study tomorrow.
extraExamples.explanation: Va matches Ana. Mañana supplies the future time.

contrast.title: A destination or a future action?

items.explanation: A place after a describes movement.
An infinitive after a describes a future action or intention.

closerLook.title: Future does not have to mean immediate
closerLook.body: Voy a viajar el año que viene is possible. The construction is common for plans and expectations, not restricted to the next few minutes.

closerLook.title: Another way to discuss plans
closerLook.body: The present can describe scheduled plans: Mañana trabajo. The simple future has its own uses and is covered separately.

mistakes.explanation: Keep a between ir and the infinitive.
Only ir is conjugated in this pattern.

practice.prompt: Say: I am going to read.
practice.explanation: Voy + a + infinitive.

practice.prompt: Say: they are going to eat.
practice.explanation: Van matches they; comer stays unchanged.

practice.prompt: Is Voy a casa a future-action construction?
practice.explanation: Casa is a destination, not an infinitive.

takeaways: Conjugate ir, keep a, then use the infinitive.
Match ir to the person making the plan.
Distinguish destinations from planned actions.

preterite.bigIdea: The preterite presents a past event as bounded or completed. It is a way to frame an event, not a rule that the event must have been short or happened only once.
preterite.goal: Form regular preterites and use them for completed events and sequences.

build.title: Choose a completed viewpoint
build.body: Ayer trabajé puts yesterday’s work inside a completed time frame. Viví allí diez años can describe a long period viewed as a whole.

build.title: Build regular forms
build.body: For -ar: -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron. For -er/-ir: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. Keep written accents: hablé, comió.

build.title: Move a story forward
build.body: Llegué, abrí la puerta y entré presents a sequence of completed events. Use each verb to advance the narrative.

extraExamples.english: I lived in Madrid for ten years.
extraExamples.explanation: A long period can use the preterite when viewed as a completed whole.

extraExamples.english: I arrived, had dinner and went to bed.
extraExamples.explanation: The completed events move the story forward in sequence.

items.explanation: The preterite presents the reading as completed.

items.english: I was reading when you called.
items.explanation: The imperfect frames reading as ongoing background.

closerLook.title: Common irregulars
closerLook.body: Ir and ser share fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron. Context distinguishes went from was/were. Tener uses tuve; hacer uses hice.

closerLook.title: Spelling preserves sound
closerLook.body: Buscar becomes busqué in yo, with qu keeping the k sound before é. Do not mechanically append endings without checking spelling.

mistakes.explanation: Present hablo and preterite hablé are different forms.

mistakes.incorrect: A long event must use the imperfect.
mistakes.correct: A completed long event can use the preterite.
mistakes.explanation: Duration alone does not determine the viewpoint.

practice.prompt: Say: yesterday I spoke with Ana.
practice.explanation: A completed event takes hablé, with its accent.

practice.prompt: Say: we ate at two.
practice.explanation: The regular -er nosotros preterite ends in -imos.

practice.prompt: Can Viví allí veinte años use the preterite?
practice.explanation: The twenty years can be presented as a completed period.

takeaways: Use preterite for events viewed as completed wholes.
Duration alone does not choose the tense.
Learn irregular forms and preserve accent marks.

imperfect.bigIdea: The imperfect places you inside a past situation without presenting its endpoint. It is useful for habits, descriptions and actions in progress—the setting around events.
imperfect.goal: Describe past routines and background with regular imperfect forms.

build.title: Describe the background
build.body: Era tarde and Hacía frío set the scene. The imperfect does not tell you where the situation began or ended.

build.title: Describe repeated activity
build.body: De niño jugaba aquí describes a childhood habit. English might use used to, would, or a simple past translation.

build.title: Build the forms
build.body: For -ar use -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban. For -er/-ir use -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. The main irregular verbs are ser, ir and ver.

extraExamples.spanish: De niña, vivía cerca del mar.
extraExamples.english: As a child, I lived near the sea.
extraExamples.explanation: Vivía describes a past situation without packaging it as a completed period.

extraExamples.english: It was eight o’clock and it was raining.
extraExamples.explanation: Time and weather establish the background.

contrast.title: View the action from inside or as a whole

items.english: I was reading when you arrived.
items.explanation: Reading is the ongoing background.
The preterite presents a completed amount of reading.

closerLook.title: The main irregulars
closerLook.body: Ser: era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran. Ir: iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban. Ver: veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían.

closerLook.title: Repeated does not always mean imperfect
closerLook.body: Fui tres veces presents three visits as a completed set. Repetition helps suggest a habit but does not force the imperfect.

mistakes.explanation: The -aba set belongs to -ar verbs; comer takes -ía.

mistakes.incorrect: Every repeated action requires the imperfect.
mistakes.correct: A completed set can use the preterite.
mistakes.explanation: The viewpoint matters more than counting repetitions.

practice.prompt: Say: we used to speak every day.
practice.explanation: Use the imperfect for a past routine; keep the accent.

practice.prompt: Complete: Cuando era niño, __ aquí. (vivir, yo)
practice.explanation: An ongoing childhood situation uses the imperfect.

practice.prompt: Must three completed visits be imperfect?
practice.answer: No: Fui tres veces is possible.
practice.explanation: The visits can be grouped as a completed set.

takeaways: Use imperfect for background, habits and actions viewed from inside.
Regular -ar uses -aba; -er/-ir use -ía.
A time word alone does not mechanically choose a tense.

past-contrast.bigIdea: Preterite and imperfect offer different viewpoints on the past. One presents an event as a whole; the other shows the situation from inside. A story often needs both.
past-contrast.goal: Choose a tense by narrative role rather than by event length.

build.title: Separate event from setting
build.body: Llovía cuando salí means it was raining when I left. Llovía gives the setting; salí marks the event.

build.title: Choose your viewpoint
build.body: Vivía en Madrid gives background. Viví en Madrid diez años presents a completed period. The real-life situation can be similar while the storytelling changes.

build.title: Use interruptions as a model, not a law
build.body: Dormía cuando sonó el teléfono is a useful pattern. But not every preterite interrupts an imperfect, and not every imperfect needs an interruption.

extraExamples.english: We were walking when it started to rain.
extraExamples.explanation: Caminábamos supplies ongoing background; empezó introduces a new event.

extraExamples.english: I worked there for five years.
extraExamples.explanation: A long period is presented as completed; length does not require imperfect.

items.spanish: Cuando llegué, Ana preparaba la cena.
items.english: When I arrived, Ana was preparing dinner.
items.explanation: Preparation was already in progress.

items.spanish: Cuando llegué, Ana preparó la cena.
items.english: When I arrived, Ana prepared dinner.
items.explanation: Preparation is presented as a completed event in the narrative, naturally read as following the arrival.

closerLook.title: Meaning effects
closerLook.body: Sabía means knew; supe can mean found out. Conocía describes knowing someone; conocí can describe meeting them. Viewpoint can produce different natural English translations.

closerLook.title: Time expressions give clues
closerLook.body: Siempre and ayer are context, not automatic switches. Ayer llovía cuando salí is perfectly possible.

mistakes.incorrect: Long action = imperfect, short action = preterite.
mistakes.correct: Choose by viewpoint and narrative role.
mistakes.explanation: Both tenses can describe events of many durations.

mistakes.incorrect: Ayer forces every verb into the preterite.
mistakes.explanation: A past day can contain both background and completed events.

practice.prompt: Complete: __ cuando sonó el teléfono. (I was sleeping)
practice.explanation: Sleeping is the ongoing background.

practice.prompt: Complete: Dormía cuando __ el teléfono. (ring)
practice.explanation: The ringing is presented as the event.

practice.prompt: Explain vivía versus viví en Madrid.
practice.answer: Vivía supplies background; viví presents a completed stay.
practice.explanation: The choice frames the information differently.

takeaways: Preterite packages events as wholes.
Imperfect gives an inside view or background.
Choose based on what the sentence is doing in the story.

future.bigIdea: The simple future can describe future events, predictions and promises. It can also express a guess about the present, so its meaning comes from context as well as its name.
future.goal: Attach future endings to an infinitive and recognize common irregular stems.

build.title: Keep the infinitive
build.body: For regular verbs, start with the whole infinitive: hablar-, comer-, vivir-. Do not remove the final -ar, -er or -ir.

build.title: Use one set of endings
build.body: Add -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án: hablaré, hablarás, hablará, hablaremos, hablaréis, hablarán. The same endings work for all three families.

build.title: Read the context
build.body: Te llamaré mañana is a future promise. ¿Dónde estará Ana? can mean I wonder where Ana is now, with future morphology expressing conjecture.

extraExamples.explanation: Llamar + -é identifies yo and presents a future action.
Comer stays whole before -emos.

items.english: Ana will be at home tomorrow.
items.explanation: Mañana places the situation in the future.

items.english: Where is Ana? She is probably at home.
items.explanation: The future form expresses a present guess in this context.

closerLook.title: Irregular stems keep the same endings
closerLook.body: Tener → tendr-, poder → podr-, salir → saldr-, hacer → har-, decir → dir-. For example, tendré and haré.

closerLook.title: Choose among natural future expressions
closerLook.body: Voy a llamar often expresses an intention. Llamaré can express a promise or prediction. The present also works for some scheduled events.

mistakes.explanation: The future keeps the infinitive; hablé is preterite.
Tener uses the irregular future stem tendr-.

practice.prompt: Say: we will live here.
practice.explanation: Add -emos to vivir.

practice.prompt: Say: I will have time.
practice.explanation: Use tendr- + -é.

practice.prompt: In response to Where is Ana now, what can Estará en casa mean?
practice.explanation: The future can express conjecture about the present.

takeaways: Regular future endings attach to the whole infinitive.
Irregular stems use the same ending set.
Context distinguishes a future event from a present guess.

conditional.bigIdea: The conditional lets you describe an imagined result, make a request more tentative, or speak about a future viewed from the past. It often corresponds to English would.
conditional.goal: Form regular conditionals and distinguish their main uses.

build.title: Attach endings to the infinitive
build.body: Add -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían to the full infinitive: hablaría, comerías, viviríamos.

build.title: Frame an imagined result
build.body: Con más tiempo, viajaría means with more time, I would travel. The condition can be stated as a phrase rather than a full si clause.

build.title: Make a request tentative
build.body: ¿Podrías ayudarme? means could you help me? The conditional softens the request; it does not necessarily describe a future event.

extraExamples.spanish: Con más dinero, compraría una casa.
extraExamples.english: With more money, I would buy a house.
extraExamples.explanation: Compraría presents an imagined result.

extraExamples.english: She said she would arrive late.
extraExamples.explanation: Llegaría is future relative to the past moment dijo.

items.explanation: Future presents a future event.

items.english: I would travel with more time.
items.explanation: Conditional presents a result dependent on circumstances.

closerLook.title: Share irregular stems with the future
closerLook.body: Tener → tendría, poder → podría, hacer → haría, decir → diría. The stem changes match the simple future.

closerLook.title: A common si pattern
closerLook.body: Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría uses imperfect subjunctive in the condition and conditional in the result. Do not automatically put the conditional after si.

mistakes.explanation: In this hypothetical pattern, the si clause uses imperfect subjunctive.

mistakes.incorrect: hablaba for I would speak in an imagined result
mistakes.explanation: Hablaba is imperfect; hablaría is conditional.

practice.prompt: Say: we would eat here.
practice.explanation: Keep comer and add -íamos.

practice.prompt: Make Can you help me? more tentative with poder and tú.
practice.explanation: Podrías uses the irregular stem podr-.

practice.prompt: Complete: Dijo que __ tarde. (would arrive)
practice.explanation: This is future viewed from a past reference point.

takeaways: Conditional endings attach to the infinitive.
Use it for imagined results, tentative requests and future-in-the-past.
A hypothetical si clause usually needs a different form.

subjunctive.bigIdea: The subjunctive is a grammatical mood used in particular constructions. It often presents a desired, evaluated or unconfirmed situation instead of asserting it as a fact. “Uncertain” alone is not a complete rule.
subjunctive.goal: Recognize three common triggers and build regular present subjunctive forms.

build.title: Start with the whole expression
build.body: Quiero que vengas expresses a wish about someone else. Es importante que estudies evaluates an action. No creo que sea verdad does not assert the following idea as true.

build.title: Build regular forms
build.body: Use the present yo stem and swap vowel families: hablar → hable, hables, hable, hablemos, habléis, hablen; comer/vivir → coma/viva, comas/vivas, coma/viva, comamos/vivamos, comáis/viváis, coman/vivan.

build.title: Check who performs each action
build.body: Quiero estudiar means I want to study. Quiero que estudies means I want you to study. A different subject commonly leads to que + a conjugated verb.

extraExamples.explanation: Espero que presents a desired situation; tener has the subjunctive form tengas.

extraExamples.english: It is important that you arrive early.
extraExamples.explanation: The evaluation es importante que calls for the subjunctive here.

contrast.title: Assert a belief or withhold it

items.explanation: An affirmative belief normally uses indicative tiene.

items.english: I do not think she has time.
items.explanation: The negated belief normally uses subjunctive tenga.

closerLook.title: Important irregulars
closerLook.body: Ser → sea, ir → vaya, estar → esté, saber → sepa, dar → dé. Stem-changing and spelling-changing verbs require extra attention.

closerLook.title: Que is not a trigger by itself
closerLook.body: Sé que viene uses indicative because it asserts knowledge. Learn governing expressions rather than treating every que as a command to change mood.

mistakes.explanation: The wish about the listener requires the subjunctive here.
An assertion of knowledge normally takes indicative.

practice.prompt: Complete: Quiero que __. (hablar, tú)
practice.explanation: The wish about tú uses present subjunctive.

practice.prompt: Say: I want to study.
practice.explanation: The same intended actor allows an infinitive.

practice.prompt: Does every clause after que use the subjunctive?
practice.explanation: The governing expression and meaning determine mood.

takeaways: Learn subjunctive in complete constructions.
Wishes, evaluations and negated beliefs provide useful starting patterns.
Do not equate que or uncertainty with an automatic mood choice.

word-order.bigIdea: Spanish often uses subject–verb–object order, but the subject can disappear when the verb makes it clear. Other word orders help organize emphasis and information.
word-order.goal: Build a neutral sentence and distinguish a subject from an object.

build.title: Name the roles
build.body: In Ana compra pan, Ana is the subject, compra is the verb and pan is the direct object. Ask who buys and what is bought.

build.title: Start with a neutral order
build.body: Subject + verb + object is a dependable beginning: Luis lee un libro. Add time or place where needed: Luis lee un libro en casa.

build.title: Leave out a clear subject
build.body: Compro pan is complete: compro identifies yo. Spanish does not require an explicit subject pronoun in every sentence.

build.title: Unpack a longer sentence from the main action
build.body: In Encontraron a una niña que sostenía una vela, first find encontraron and its implied plural subject. Then find the object a una niña. Finally attach que sostenía una vela as a description of niña. A second verb need not be a second main action.

build.title: Check a person’s role before interpreting a
build.body: Veo a Ana uses personal a with a specific human direct object. Le doy agua a Ana uses a Ana as the recipient. Both contain a, but Ana has different roles. Specificity, verb meaning and construction matter; not every person noun automatically takes a.

extraExamples.spanish: Ana compra pan en el mercado.
extraExamples.english: Ana buys bread at the market.
extraExamples.explanation: Subject, verb, object and place appear in a neutral order.

extraExamples.spanish: Leo un libro por la noche.
extraExamples.english: I read a book at night.
extraExamples.explanation: The subject yo is supplied by leo; the time phrase comes afterward.

items.explanation: This is a neutral statement about Ana.
Putting mañana first frames the time; final Ana can supply the arriving person as new information.

closerLook.title: Pronouns have their own positions
closerLook.body: Lo leo means I read it. A direct-object pronoun normally comes before a conjugated verb, even though a full noun object commonly follows it.

closerLook.title: People as direct objects
closerLook.body: Veo a Ana includes the personal a before a specific person. That a does not make Ana the subject.

closerLook.title: The subject can follow the verb
closerLook.body: Llegó una señora and faltaban los registros place the subject after the verb. Use agreement and meaning to find who or what belongs with the verb; do not assume the first noun is always the subject.

mistakes.incorrect: Yo un libro leo. as a neutral beginner pattern
mistakes.explanation: Start with subject–verb–object before exploring marked word orders.

mistakes.incorrect: Adding yo to every sentence as a requirement
mistakes.explanation: The verb can identify the subject.

practice.prompt: Put in neutral order: pan / compra / Ana.
practice.explanation: Subject, verb, direct object.

practice.prompt: Who is the subject in Comemos arroz?
practice.explanation: The verb ending identifies we.

practice.prompt: In Veo a Ana, is Ana the subject?
practice.answer: No, Ana is the direct object.
practice.explanation: The speaker does the seeing.

takeaways: Use subject–verb–object as a starting point.
Let verb endings identify clear subjects.
Word order can organize emphasis and new information.

questions.bigIdea: A question starts with a gap. Sometimes you check whether something is true; sometimes you need a missing detail. Decide which answer you want before choosing the structure.
questions.goal: Build yes/no and information questions without importing English’s helper do.

build.title: Turn a statement into a question
build.body: Hablas español becomes ¿Hablas español? Keep the words, add question marks, and use question intonation. A neutral yes/no question often rises at the end, though patterns vary.

build.title: Ask for the missing detail
build.body: Use qué for what, dónde for where, cuándo for when, cómo for how, quién for who and por qué for why. A useful pattern is question word + conjugated verb + the rest.

build.title: Match the person
build.body: ¿Dónde vives? addresses tú. ¿Dónde vive Ana? asks about Ana. The verb still matches its subject; a named subject commonly follows the verb in this pattern.

build.title: Keep the marks and accents
build.body: Write ¿…? around the question and keep the accents on question words. In Ana, ¿dónde vives?, the question begins after the name.

extraExamples.explanation: Tienes already means you have; Spanish does not add a helper equivalent to do.
Vive agrees with Ana. The question word requests a place.

contrast.title: Change one word. Change the gap.

items.explanation: Dónde asks for a place: Trabajo en un hospital.
Cuándo asks for a time: Trabajo los lunes.

closerLook.title: Talking to Ana or about her?
closerLook.body: ¿Dónde vive Ana? asks about Ana. Ana, ¿dónde vives? addresses her directly. The comma and verb ending help distinguish the messages.

closerLook.title: An accent beyond question marks
closerLook.body: ¿Dónde trabajas? asks for a place; Trabajo donde vivo connects ideas without a question. An indirect question keeps the accent: No sé dónde vive Ana.

closerLook.title: Por qué asks; porque answers
closerLook.body: ¿Por qué estudias español? asks why. Porque me gusta answers because I like it. Why is two words with an accent; because is one word without one.

closerLook.title: Including tú
closerLook.body: ¿Dónde vives? is complete. ¿Dónde vives tú? can add contrast: Yo vivo en Madrid. ¿Dónde vives tú?

mistakes.explanation: Haces is not an English-style question helper. Hablas is enough.
Use a conjugated verb, not the infinitive.
The question word needs its written accent.

practice.prompt: Turn Tienes un perro into a yes/no question.
practice.explanation: Keep the words and add question marks and question intonation.

practice.prompt: Your friend says Trabajo en una escuela. Ask where they work.
practice.explanation: Dónde requests the place; trabajas addresses your friend, while trabajo describes the speaker.

practice.prompt: Ask where Ana lives.
practice.explanation: Ana is the subject, so use vive, not vives.

takeaways: Decide whether you need yes/no or a missing detail.
Match the verb to the person the question is about.
Add ¿…? and keep the accents on question words.

negatives.bigIdea: Spanish normally puts no before a conjugated verb to make a negative statement. Words such as nada and nadie can work with no without canceling the negative meaning.
negatives.goal: Negate a sentence and use common negative words in their usual positions.

build.title: Put no before the verb
build.body: Trabajo becomes No trabajo. Spanish does not add an English-style do not helper.

build.title: Keep pronouns between no and the verb
build.body: Lo veo becomes No lo veo. Me levanto becomes No me levanto. No comes before the whole pronoun-and-verb group.

build.title: Choose negative words
build.body: Nada means nothing/not anything; nadie means nobody/not anybody; nunca means never. After the verb, these normally accompany no: No veo nada.

extraExamples.explanation: No goes directly before tengo.
The object pronoun lo stays between no and entiendo.

contrast.title: The position changes the need for no

items.explanation: Nadie follows the verb, so no appears before it.
Nadie before the verb already supplies the negation.

closerLook.title: Negative concord is normal
closerLook.body: No veo nada means I do not see anything. It is standard Spanish, not an accidental positive made from two negatives.

closerLook.title: Negation can target another part
closerLook.body: No todos vienen means not everyone is coming. This is different from Nadie viene, which means nobody is coming.

mistakes.explanation: Ordinary sentence negation places no before the verb.
A preverbal nadie normally supplies negation without no.

practice.prompt: Negate Tengo hambre.
practice.explanation: Place no before tengo.

practice.prompt: Negate Lo veo.
practice.explanation: No comes before the object pronoun.

practice.prompt: Say I do not see anything.
practice.explanation: Postverbal nada combines with no.

takeaways: Place no before the conjugated verb group.
Nada and nadie after the verb normally accompany no.
Negative concord is standard Spanish.

connecting.bigIdea: Connecting words tell the reader how two ideas relate. Choose the relationship first—addition, contrast, reason or result—then choose the connector.
connecting.goal: Join clauses with y, pero, porque and por eso while preserving their meaning.

build.title: Add or contrast
build.body: Y adds related information: Trabajo y estudio. Pero introduces a contrast: Quiero ir, pero no puedo.

build.title: Give a reason
build.body: Porque introduces why: Estudio porque tengo un examen. The reason follows porque.

build.title: Give a result
build.body: Por eso points to a consequence: Tengo un examen; por eso estudio. Notice how reversing the clauses changes which connector makes sense.

extraExamples.english: I want to go out, but it is raining.
extraExamples.explanation: Pero signals a contrast between the wish and the situation.

extraExamples.english: I am hungry; that is why I cook.
extraExamples.explanation: Por eso introduces the result of being hungry.

items.english: I study because I have an exam.
items.explanation: Porque introduces the reason.

items.spanish: Tengo un examen; por eso estudio.
items.english: I have an exam; that is why I study.
items.explanation: Por eso introduces the consequence.

closerLook.title: Y sometimes becomes e
closerLook.body: Before an i sound, y usually changes to e: español e inglés. The change follows sound, with exceptions such as y hielo, where the next word starts with a glide.

closerLook.title: Pero versus sino
closerLook.body: No quiero té, sino café corrects an alternative: not tea but coffee. Pero simply contrasts two ideas.

mistakes.explanation: The question why uses two words and an accent; porque introduces an answer or reason.

mistakes.incorrect: No quiero té, pero café. for not tea but coffee
mistakes.explanation: Sino supplies a correction after a negative.

practice.prompt: Join: I want to go / I cannot, showing contrast.
practice.explanation: Pero marks the contrast.

practice.prompt: Complete: Estudio __ tengo un examen.
practice.explanation: The second clause supplies the reason.

practice.prompt: Complete: español __ inglés.
practice.explanation: Y changes to e before the initial i sound.

takeaways: Choose the logical relationship before the connector.
Porque introduces a reason; por eso introduces a result.
Use sino to correct an alternative after a negative.

por-para.bigIdea: Por and para both translate as for in some sentences, but they express several different relationships. Learn those relationships rather than assigning one English word to each.
por-para.goal: Distinguish common purpose, recipient, cause, exchange and route patterns.

build.title: Use para for a goal
build.body: Estudio para aprender gives a purpose. Salgo para Madrid points to a destination. Es para Ana identifies an intended recipient.

build.title: Use por for a cause or path
build.body: Lo hago por ti gives a motivating reason or someone’s sake. Camino por el parque describes a route through an area.

build.title: Recognize exchange and deadlines
build.body: Pago diez euros por el libro uses por for an exchange. Lo necesito para el lunes uses para for a deadline.

extraExamples.explanation: Para names the intended recipient.

extraExamples.spanish: Pagamos veinte euros por la cena.
extraExamples.english: We paid twenty euros for dinner.
extraExamples.explanation: Por marks what the money is exchanged for.

items.explanation: Para highlights you as the intended beneficiary or recipient.

items.english: I do it for your sake.
items.explanation: Por highlights you as the motivating reason.

closerLook.title: Useful fixed expressions
closerLook.body: Por ejemplo, por favor and para siempre are learned as whole expressions. Their meanings are not reliably reconstructed from English for.

closerLook.title: A shortcut with limits
closerLook.body: Purpose versus cause is a useful contrast, but it does not cover routes, exchanges, recipients and every fixed expression. Ask what relationship is being expressed.

mistakes.incorrect: Estudio por aprender. for in order to learn
mistakes.explanation: Para + infinitive is the purpose pattern here.

mistakes.incorrect: Pago diez euros para el libro.
mistakes.correct: Pago diez euros por el libro.
mistakes.explanation: The book is the item received in exchange.

practice.prompt: Complete: Este regalo es __ ti.
practice.explanation: You are naming the recipient.

practice.prompt: Complete: Caminamos __ el parque.
practice.explanation: You are describing the route through an area.

practice.prompt: Say: I need it by Monday.
practice.explanation: Para introduces this deadline.

takeaways: Para often points toward a purpose, destination, recipient or deadline.
Por often marks cause, route or exchange.
Learn fixed expressions as units.

gustar.bigIdea: Gustar is easiest to understand as “be pleasing to.” The liked thing controls the verb; a small pronoun tells you who experiences the liking.
gustar.goal: Choose gusta or gustan and match the experiencer pronoun.

build.title: Start with the thing liked
build.body: Me gusta el libro is structurally the book is pleasing to me. El libro is the subject of gusta, even though English says I like the book.

build.title: Match singular or plural
build.body: Use gusta with a singular noun or an infinitive: Me gusta el café; Me gusta leer. Use gustan with a plural noun: Me gustan los libros.

build.title: Choose who experiences it
build.body: Use me, te, le, nos, os, les. Le can mean to him, her or you formal; les can mean to them or you plural.

extraExamples.explanation: The infinitive cocinar takes singular gusta; nos names the people who like it.

extraExamples.spanish: A Ana le gustan las películas.
extraExamples.explanation: Plural películas takes gustan. A Ana clarifies who le refers to.

contrast.title: The number belongs to the liked thing

items.explanation: One book takes gusta.
Plural books take gustan; me stays unchanged.

closerLook.title: Clarifying and emphasizing
closerLook.body: A mí me gusta can emphasize the experiencer. A Ana le gusta clarifies le. Keep the small pronoun in these ordinary constructions.

closerLook.title: Similar verbs
closerLook.body: Encantar and interesar often follow a similar pattern: Me encantan estos libros; Me interesa la historia. Learn meaning and agreement together.

mistakes.explanation: Café, not yo, controls the verb.
The plural subject requires gustan.

practice.prompt: Say: I like the houses.
practice.explanation: Casas is plural, so use gustan.

practice.prompt: Say: we like reading.
practice.explanation: Nos identifies we; an infinitive takes gusta.

practice.prompt: Complete: A Ana __ gusta el café.
practice.explanation: Ana is the experiencer, represented by le.

takeaways: The liked thing controls gusta/gustan.
The pronoun identifies the experiencer.
Use gusta with an infinitive.

commands.bigIdea: Commands ask someone to act or not act. Spanish changes the form for the person addressed, and a negative tú command does not simply add no to the affirmative form.
commands.goal: Build common tú and usted commands and place attached pronouns correctly.

build.title: Start with affirmative tú
build.body: For a regular verb, the form matches the present él/ella form: habla, come, vive. Common irregulars include di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten and ven.

build.title: Change the pattern for no
build.body: Negative tú uses present subjunctive: no hables, no comas, no vivas. Keep the final s in these forms.

build.title: Use subjunctive forms for usted
build.body: Hable, coma, viva address usted; no hable, no coma, no viva are negative. Plural ustedes uses hablen, coman, vivan.

extraExamples.explanation: Abre is an affirmative tú command from abrir.
Negative tú uses abras, the subjunctive form.

contrast.title: Affirmative and negative change pronoun position

items.explanation: An affirmative command attaches lo to the verb; the accent preserves stress.
A negative command puts lo before the verb and uses leas.

closerLook.title: Politeness is more than verb choice
closerLook.body: Usted commands can sound formal, but tone, context and por favor matter too. ¿Podrías ayudarme? offers a more tentative request.

closerLook.title: Affirmative tú is not always regular
closerLook.body: Ven aquí uses the irregular command of venir. Do not assume every command equals a regular present form.

mistakes.incorrect: No habla. when telling tú not to speak
mistakes.explanation: Use the negative tú subjunctive form.

mistakes.incorrect: Lo lee. for Read it! to tú
mistakes.explanation: Attach the pronoun to the affirmative command and preserve stress.

practice.prompt: Tell a friend: speak slowly.
practice.explanation: Use affirmative tú habla.

practice.prompt: Tell a friend: do not speak.
practice.explanation: Negative tú uses hables.

practice.prompt: Make Léelo negative for tú.
practice.explanation: Move lo before the verb and use leas.

takeaways: Choose the addressee and affirmative/negative pattern.
Negative tú uses the subjunctive.
Attach pronouns to affirmative commands; place them before negative ones.
