accent-marks.bigIdea: A spoken word has stress; a written accent is a spelling mark. The acute accent in á/é/í/ó/ú is commonly called a tilde in Spanish. It can indicate exceptional stress, a stressed closed vowel in a hiatus, or a grammatical distinction. The sign over ñ is different: it identifies a letter and does not mark stress.
accent-marks.goal: Explain a stress accent and recognize common meaning-distinguishing accents.

build.title: Classify where the stress falls
build.body: Agudas stress the last syllable: ca-fé. Llanas stress the next-to-last: CA-sa. Esdrújulas stress the third-to-last: te-LÉ-fo-no. Start with syllables, not a count of letters.

build.title: Apply the usual spelling rules
build.body: An aguda normally takes an accent if it ends in a vowel, n or s: café, canción; hotel needs none. A llana normally takes an accent if it does not end in a vowel, n or s: lápiz; casa needs none. Esdrújulas and words stressed earlier take accents. Special consonant clusters and vowel sequences need additional rules.

build.title: Recognize distinguishing accents
build.body: Tú means you; tu means your. Él means he; el means the. Sí means yes; si means if. Mí is a pronoun; mi is a possessive. These diacritic accents distinguish roles rather than simply increasing loudness.

build.title: Check vowel combinations and question words
build.body: Día and río have a stressed closed vowel and separate syllables. Qué, quién, cómo, dónde and cuándo take accents when interrogative or exclamatory, including indirect questions such as No sé dónde está.

extraExamples.explanation: Subject tú has an accent; possessive tu does not.

extraExamples.english: Yes, I will go if I have time.
extraExamples.explanation: Sí is yes; si introduces a condition.

items.explanation: Él is a subject pronoun.
El is a definite article.

closerLook.title: Accents can separate vowel sounds
closerLook.body: In día, the accent on the weak vowel í helps signal a hiatus: dí-a. Accent rules involve syllable structure as well as the default stress pattern.

closerLook.title: Forms can gain or lose a mark
closerLook.body: Canción becomes canciones without an accent because the default plural stress is already correct. Preserve the pronunciation, not the mark mechanically.

closerLook.title: A mark can appear or disappear when forms change
closerLook.body: Canción becomes canciones: the plural’s default stress is already correct. Attaching pronouns can require a mark: lee → léelo. Preserve the intended stress rather than copying or deleting marks mechanically.

closerLook.title: Emphasis does not decide spelling
closerLook.body: Do not add an acute accent because a word is important or spoken loudly. The tilde on a vowel follows orthographic rules; the sign in ñ identifies a consonant letter.

closerLook.title: Short words and -mente adverbs
closerLook.body: Monosyllables normally have no written accent: fue, vio and dio. Diacritic pairs such as tú/tu are specific exceptions, not a reason to accent every short word. Adverbs in -mente preserve the adjective’s written accent: rápida → rápidamente; clara → claramente. They need separate treatment rather than mechanical application of the ordinary word-stress shortcut.

mistakes.explanation: The subject pronoun tú needs an accent.
The plural’s default stress already falls on the correct syllable.

practice.prompt: Why does café need an accent but hotel does not?
practice.answer: Both are agudas; café ends in a vowel, hotel in l.
practice.explanation: The final-stress spelling rules differ by ending.

practice.prompt: Why does lápiz need an accent but casa does not?
practice.answer: Both are llanas; lápiz ends in z, casa in a vowel.
practice.explanation: Llanas normally take an accent outside vowel/n/s endings.

practice.prompt: Does making yo emphatic in Yo hablo require changing hablo to habló?
practice.explanation: Habló is a different verb form, not an emphatic spelling of hablo.

takeaways: Accents can signal exceptional stress or grammatical distinctions.
Learn common pairs in complete phrases.
Recheck spelling when a word changes form.

punctuation.bigIdea: Spanish marks direct questions and exclamations at both ends. The opening mark helps readers choose the right intonation before they reach the end.
punctuation.goal: Place opening marks at the start of the question or exclamation, including inside a longer sentence.

build.title: Mark the whole direct question
build.body: Write ¿Cómo estás? with an opening inverted question mark and a closing question mark. Do not add a full stop after the closing mark at the end of the sentence.

build.title: Mark an exclamation
build.body: ¡Qué bonito! expresses an exclamation. Exclamation words such as qué and cómo keep their written accents.

build.title: Find where the question actually starts
build.body: In Ana, ¿vienes mañana?, the name gets someone’s attention before the question begins. The opening mark belongs before vienes.

extraExamples.explanation: The opening question mark starts the actual question, after the name.
Opening and closing exclamation marks frame the exclamation.

items.explanation: A direct question uses question marks.

items.english: I do not know where Ana is.
items.explanation: An indirect question uses no question marks here, but dónde retains its accent.

closerLook.title: Inside a longer sentence
closerLook.body: Si puedes, ¿me llamas? places the opening mark after the initial condition. Punctuation marks the scope of the question rather than automatically enclosing every preceding word.

closerLook.title: More than punctuation
closerLook.body: Writing marks cannot replace the right verb form or word choice. In speech, listeners rely on the structure and intonation instead.

mistakes.explanation: Written direct questions use an opening mark too.
Do not add a full stop after a closing question mark ending the sentence.

practice.prompt: Punctuate: Dónde vives
practice.explanation: Add both marks and retain the accent.

practice.prompt: Punctuate a greeting to Ana followed by Are you coming?: Ana vienes
practice.explanation: The name is outside the question; the comma marks direct address.

practice.prompt: Does No sé dónde está need question marks as a statement?
practice.explanation: It contains an indirect question, with an accent on dónde.

takeaways: Use opening and closing marks for direct questions and exclamations.
Place the opening mark where that part begins.
Indirect questions can keep accents without question marks.

se.bigIdea: Se is a small word with several grammatical jobs. Instead of assigning it one translation, identify the construction around it: self-directed action, a general statement, an affected person, or a pronoun combination.
se.goal: Distinguish four common se patterns using meaning and agreement.

build.title: Look for a self-directed action
build.body: Ana se lava means Ana washes herself. Se links the receiver of the action to Ana. Some verbs with se have a broader or changed meaning, such as irse.

build.title: Look for a general or passive-like statement
build.body: Se vive bien aquí means people live well here: impersonal se with a singular verb. Se venden libros is passive-like: books are sold, with plural agreement.

build.title: Check neighboring pronouns
build.body: In Se lo doy, se replaces le or les before lo/la/los/las. In Se me cayó el vaso, me identifies the affected person, while el vaso controls cayó.

extraExamples.explanation: In this passive-like construction, plural casas agrees with venden.
Se replaces le before lo; it does not mean herself.

items.explanation: Impersonal se has no expressed subject; vive stays singular.
Passive-like se has plural libros as the grammatical subject, so use venden.

closerLook.title: An affected-person pattern
closerLook.body: Se me cayó el vaso means I dropped the glass / the glass fell on me. Caerse describes the event; me marks the affected person. The construction can downplay agency without guaranteeing an accident.

closerLook.title: A personal object stays singular in the impersonal pattern
closerLook.body: Se busca a los responsables uses a personal object with a, not a plural subject; busca stays singular. Contrast Se buscan empleados, where empleados agrees with buscan.

mistakes.explanation: Le/les changes to se before lo/la/los/las.
In this passive-like construction, casas is plural and controls the verb.

practice.prompt: Classify Ana se lava.
practice.explanation: Ana does the washing and receives it.

practice.prompt: Complete: Se __ libros. (vender, passive-like)
practice.explanation: Plural libros requires plural agreement.

practice.prompt: Why does le become se in Se lo doy?
practice.explanation: This se is a pronoun replacement, not a reflexive marker.

takeaways: Identify the construction before translating se.
Impersonal and passive-like patterns differ in agreement.
Se can replace le/les or occur in affected-person constructions.

hypotheticals.bigIdea: Conditional sentences connect a possible situation with its result. Spanish changes the verb pattern depending on whether the condition is treated as open, imagined or contrary to a completed past.
hypotheticals.goal: Distinguish open conditions, imagined present/future conditions and unreal past conditions.

build.title: Leave a possibility open
build.body: Si tengo tiempo, iré means if I have time, I will go. The si clause uses present indicative, even though the situation concerns the future.

build.title: Imagine a different present or future
build.body: Si tuviera tiempo, iría means if I had time, I would go. Use imperfect subjunctive in the condition and conditional in the result.

build.title: Imagine a different completed past
build.body: Si hubiera tenido tiempo, habría ido means if I had had time, I would have gone. Use pluperfect subjunctive for the condition and conditional perfect for the result.

extraExamples.spanish: Si llueve, nos quedaremos en casa.
extraExamples.english: If it rains, we will stay at home.
extraExamples.explanation: An open future possibility uses present llueve after si and future in the result.

extraExamples.english: If I had studied, I would have passed.
extraExamples.explanation: The speaker imagines a different completed past, using compound forms.

items.english: If I have time, I will go.
items.explanation: The condition is treated as open.

items.english: If I had time, I would go.
items.explanation: The speaker takes a more hypothetical stance toward having time.

closerLook.title: Form the imperfect subjunctive
closerLook.body: Start with the preterite ellos form, remove -ron and add -ra endings: tuvieron → tuviera. The -se series, such as tuviese, is also standard.

closerLook.title: Results can vary
closerLook.body: Si tienes tiempo, ven uses a command as the result. Si tengo tiempo, voy can use the present. Mixed-time hypotheticals also exist; choose a pattern by meaning rather than memorizing one mandatory result tense.

mistakes.explanation: An ordinary open future condition uses present indicative after si.
This imagined-condition pattern uses imperfect subjunctive in the si clause.

practice.prompt: Complete an open condition: Si __ tiempo, iré. (tener, yo)
practice.explanation: Use present indicative for an open future condition.

practice.prompt: Complete an imagined condition: Si tuviera tiempo, __. (go, yo)
practice.explanation: The result uses the conditional in this pattern.

practice.prompt: Complete the unreal past: Si hubiera estudiado, __ aprobado.
practice.explanation: Habría + participle builds the conditional perfect result.

takeaways: Decide how the speaker frames the condition.
Open: si + present; imagined: si + imperfect subjunctive.
Unreal past commonly combines hubiera + participle with habría + participle.

letter-combinations.bigIdea: Two letters can work together to represent one consonant sound. Other letters change sound with the following vowel. Learning these patterns helps you decode unfamiliar words instead of assigning an English sound to every letter.
letter-combinations.goal: Recognize common consonant spellings in the stories, including ll.

build.title: Read ll and ch together
build.body: In llave and calle, ll represents one consonant sound, not two English l sounds. Most speakers pronounce consonantal y and ll alike, with regional variation. Ch in chico also represents one consonant sound.

build.title: Check the vowel after c and g
build.body: C before a/o/u has a k sound; before e/i it commonly has an s sound in Latin America. G before a/o/u has a hard g; before e/i it has the sound also written j. Compare casa/cine and gato/gente.

build.title: Use qu and gu to preserve a sound
build.body: Qu before e/i keeps the k sound: queso, quién. Gue/gui keep hard g: guerra, guitarra. Their u is normally silent; güe/güi make u audible, as in pingüino.

build.title: Notice silent letters and familiar-looking traps
build.body: H is normally silent: hola, hay. Spanish b and v do not form the ordinary English b/v sound contrast. Learn their shared pronunciation from Spanish audio rather than forcing an English v.

extraExamples.explanation: Gui preserves hard g; the u is silent here.
The diaeresis in güi signals a pronounced u.

contrast.title: A following vowel changes the reading

items.explanation: C before a represents a k sound.
C before i has an s sound in the Latin American model used here.

closerLook.title: Regional ll/y and c/z
closerLook.body: Some speakers distinguish ll from y; many do not. In much of Argentina and Uruguay, shared ll/y can sound sh-like or zh-like. Much of Spain distinguishes c before e/i and z from s. These are legitimate variants.

closerLook.title: Letters, sound and syllables are different
closerLook.body: Ll and ch are digraphs, not additional alphabet letters. That alphabet classification does not tell you how to pronounce them. A spelling diagram supports listening; it does not produce the sound.

closerLook.title: Use a concrete sound starting point
closerLook.body: Ch is close to the consonant in English cheese. Hard g is like the initial consonant of English go. Spanish j, and g before e/i, are often breathy or throaty sounds rather than the English j of judge. B and v use the lips rather than the English teeth-on-lip v articulation; their shared sound can soften between vowels. These comparisons are starting points, not exact substitutes for Spanish audio.

mistakes.incorrect: llave with two English l sounds
mistakes.correct: llave with one ll consonant sound
mistakes.explanation: Read the pair together; follow the recording’s regional model.

mistakes.incorrect: Pronouncing every written u in queso or guitarra
mistakes.correct: Keep u silent in que/qui and gue/gui
mistakes.explanation: The u is part of the spelling that preserves k or hard g.

practice.prompt: In llave, should ll be read as two English l sounds?
practice.answer: No; it represents one consonant sound.
practice.explanation: Its pronunciation varies by region, but it is not an English doubled l.

practice.prompt: Does the u sound in queso?
practice.explanation: Qu before e/i keeps a k sound with silent u.

practice.prompt: What changes between gui and güi?
practice.answer: The diaeresis makes u audible in güi.
practice.explanation: Compare guitarra and pingüino.

takeaways: Read common letter groups together.
Check the following vowel for c and g.
Use audio for the pronunciation model, including regional variation.

syllables.bigIdea: A syllable is a spoken beat organized around a vowel sound or vowel combination. Stress makes one syllable more prominent. You can hear stress even when no accent is written.
syllables.goal: Divide common words into syllables and distinguish syllable boundaries from word stress.

build.title: Start with clear beats
build.body: Casa has ca-sa; teléfono has te-lé-fo-no. Say the whole word, then slow it down without adding extra vowels.

build.title: Keep consonant groups together when appropriate
build.body: A consonant between vowels usually starts the next syllable: ca-sa. Groups such as br and pl normally stay together: li-bro, a-plau-so. Ch, ll and rr stay together between vowels: ca-lle, pe-rro.

build.title: Find the prominent beat
build.body: Casa is CA-sa and teléfono is te-LÉ-fo-no. The stressed beat is more prominent, while unstressed vowels remain clear. Capital letters here are a teaching notation, not normal Spanish spelling.

extraExamples.explanation: Libro divides li-bro; br stays together.
Calle divides ca-lle; the ll spelling stays together.

items.explanation: Each syllable has a vowel at its center.
Two consonants can belong to one syllable.

closerLook.title: Not one syllable per written vowel
closerLook.body: Vowels may combine in one syllable: aire is ai-re. Others separate: día is dí-a. The vowel-combinations lesson explains this boundary.

closerLook.title: Stress is not shouting
closerLook.body: Prominence involves several acoustic cues. Do not swallow the other vowels or move the word’s usual stress just to emphasize it in a sentence.

mistakes.explanation: The ll digraph is not split across syllables.

mistakes.incorrect: Treating every vowel letter as a separate beat
mistakes.explanation: Two vowels can form a diphthong.

practice.prompt: Divide casa into syllables.
practice.explanation: One consonant between vowels usually begins the next syllable.

practice.prompt: Divide libro into syllables.
practice.explanation: The br group stays together.

practice.prompt: Must a word have a written accent to have stress?
practice.explanation: Casa has stress on ca without an accent mark.

takeaways: Find spoken beats before applying stress rules.
Keep groups such as br and digraphs such as ll together.
A written accent and spoken stress are different concepts.

vowel-combinations.bigIdea: Two vowel letters do not always mean two syllables. A diphthong shares a syllable; a hiatus separates vowels into different syllables. This affects both pronunciation and accent spelling.
vowel-combinations.goal: Recognize common diphthongs and explain the accents in día and río.

build.title: Know the useful vowel groups
build.body: A, e and o are open vowels. I and u are closed vowels. An unstressed closed vowel next to an open vowel often shares its syllable: aire is ai-re and ciudad is ciu-dad.

build.title: Separate two open vowels
build.body: Two open vowels normally form separate syllables: teatro is te-a-tro and leer is le-er. Do not compress them merely because they are adjacent.

build.title: Notice stressed í and ú
build.body: A stressed closed vowel next to an open vowel forms a hiatus and carries an accent: día is dí-a; río is rí-o. In canción, the accent falls on the open vowel and does not break the diphthong.

extraExamples.english: We are going to the theater.
extraExamples.explanation: Teatro has three syllables: te-a-tro.
Leer has two vowel beats: le-er.

contrast.title: A closed vowel can share or separate

items.explanation: Hacia divides ha-cia; ia shares a syllable.
Hacía divides ha-cí-a; stressed í separates from a and changes the verb form.

closerLook.title: A mark does not always split vowels
closerLook.body: Canción remains can-ción. The written accent marks stress on ó, while i remains part of the same syllable.

closerLook.title: Variation and silent letters
closerLook.body: Actual speech can compress vowel sequences across words or vary in some words. Silent h does not necessarily prevent a vowel combination; spelling and pronunciation must be considered together.

mistakes.explanation: The noun needs an accent and normally has two syllables.

mistakes.incorrect: Every accent between vowels breaks a diphthong.
mistakes.explanation: An accent on an open vowel, as in canción, can leave a diphthong intact.

practice.prompt: How many syllables are in día?
practice.explanation: Stressed í separates from a.

practice.prompt: Divide teatro.
practice.explanation: Two adjacent open vowels form a hiatus.

practice.prompt: Does canción split into ci-ón because of its accent?
practice.explanation: The accented open vowel remains in the diphthong.

takeaways: Adjacent vowels can share or separate syllables.
Two open vowels normally separate.
Stressed í/ú next to an open vowel creates a marked hiatus.

sentence-emphasis.bigIdea: A word has its own stressed syllable, but a sentence also has a focus. You can highlight who acted, what happened, or a contrast without changing the spelling of the words.
sentence-emphasis.goal: Distinguish lexical stress, written accents and conversational emphasis.

build.title: Keep each word’s stress
build.body: Hablo is HA-blo even when the whole word receives extra emphasis. Saying ha-BLÓ changes the word form rather than simply adding emphasis.

build.title: Choose the contrast
build.body: Yo tengo la llave can emphasize who has it. Tengo la llave can emphasize possession in an appropriate context. Read the surrounding exchange to infer what is contrasted.

build.title: Use words and order as well as voice
build.body: Yo la tengo, no Ana makes the contrast explicit. An included subject pronoun or a phrase placed later can carry new or contrastive information; order is not a mechanical emphasis switch.

extraExamples.explanation: Hablo retains first-syllable stress regardless of which word the speaker emphasizes.
Habló is a different verb form with final stress and a written accent.

contrast.title: Focus can change without a spelling change

items.spanish: Yo tengo la llave, no Ana.
items.english: I have the key, not Ana.
items.explanation: The subject is the contrasting information.

items.spanish: Tengo la llave, no el mapa.
items.english: I have the key, not the map.
items.explanation: The object is the contrasting information.

closerLook.title: Written emphasis is not an accent rule
closerLook.body: Italics or teaching highlights may show focus. Do not add á/é/í/ó/ú just to make a word sound stronger.

closerLook.title: Listen to context
closerLook.body: A visual can point to the likely contrast, but intonation is conveyed by audio. Several readings can be possible without a surrounding conversation.

mistakes.incorrect: Adding an accent to show excitement
mistakes.explanation: Written accents follow spelling rules, not emotional intensity.

mistakes.incorrect: Moving hablo’s stress to its last syllable for emphasis
mistakes.explanation: Ha-BLÓ is a different form meaning he/she/you formal spoke.

practice.prompt: Does emphasizing yo require a new written accent?
practice.explanation: Sentence focus does not create a spelling accent.

practice.prompt: Which contrast appears in Yo tengo la llave, no Ana?
practice.explanation: The subject is contrasted with Ana.

practice.prompt: Can hablo become habló simply to sound more emphatic?
practice.explanation: That changes lexical stress and the verb form.

takeaways: Word stress stays with the word.
Sentence focus depends on contrast and context.
Do not invent written accents for emphasis.

location-prepositions.bigIdea: Location phrases answer where; movement phrases can answer where to, from, or through. Small words such as en, a and de connect a person or action to a place.
location-prepositions.goal: Read basic location and movement phrases, including multiword prepositions.

build.title: Locate something
build.body: En can locate something in or on a place; sobre often means on or above. Entre means between/among: entre dos rocas. The whole phrase gives the relationship.

build.title: Read multiword patterns together
build.body: Debajo de, detrás de, cerca de and frente a work as units. Keep the final de or a: debajo del mapa, frente a la silla.

build.title: Follow movement and origin
build.body: A often marks a destination, de an origin, hacia a direction and hasta an endpoint. A + el becomes al; de + el becomes del.

extraExamples.spanish: El río pasa entre dos rocas.
extraExamples.english: The river passes between two rocks.
extraExamples.explanation: Entre relates the river’s path to the rocks.

extraExamples.spanish: Rosa pone una vela frente a la silla.
extraExamples.english: Rosa puts a candle in front of the chair.
extraExamples.explanation: Frente a supplies the position relative to the chair.

items.explanation: En locates the speaker.

items.english: I am going to the hotel.
items.explanation: A marks the destination and contracts with el.

closerLook.title: Prepositions are not one-to-one translations
closerLook.body: En may correspond to in, on or at. Learn phrases and spatial relationships rather than matching each word to one English preposition.

closerLook.title: People and possession use some of the same words
closerLook.body: Veo a Ana uses personal a; la llave de Ana uses de for possession. A place phrase is only one use.

mistakes.explanation: Keep de in debajo de and contract de + el.

mistakes.incorrect: Voy en el hotel. for a destination
mistakes.explanation: A marks the destination here; en would need a different context.

practice.prompt: Complete: La llave está __ la mesa. (under)
practice.explanation: Debajo de keeps its de before the noun.

practice.prompt: Combine a + el puente.
practice.explanation: The article el contracts with a.

practice.prompt: What does hasta mark in Caminan hasta el río?
practice.explanation: They walk as far as the river.

takeaways: Read multiword prepositions as units.
Distinguish location, direction, endpoint and origin.
Remember al and del.

time-prepositions.bigIdea: Time phrases tell you when an event happens or how events are ordered. Spanish has its own combinations: not every English at, in or on maps to the same preposition.
time-prepositions.goal: Use common time phrases and connect an action to before or after another.

build.title: Read clock times with a
build.body: A la una is at one; a las dos is at two. Son las siete states the time; a las siete places an event at that time.

build.title: Learn days and parts of the day
build.body: El lunes can mean on Monday; los lunes means on Mondays. Por la mañana means in the morning. No English-style on is required before the day.

build.title: Connect events with an infinitive
build.body: Antes de salir means before leaving; después de comer means after eating. Al salir often means on/when leaving. The following action stays in its infinitive form.

extraExamples.spanish: Antes de salir, miro el reloj.
extraExamples.english: Before leaving, I look at the clock.
extraExamples.explanation: Antes de takes an infinitive when the actor is understood.

extraExamples.spanish: Al salir, Inés miró el río.
extraExamples.english: On leaving, Inés looked at the river.
extraExamples.explanation: Al + infinitive frames one event in relation to another.

contrast.title: Tell the time or schedule an event

items.explanation: This states the time.

items.spanish: El tren sale a las ocho.
items.explanation: A las attaches the clock time to an action.

closerLook.title: How long is a separate question
closerLook.body: Durante dos horas describes a span; desde las ocho gives a starting point. The duration lesson explains ongoing spans and reference times.

closerLook.title: A clause can introduce its own actor
closerLook.body: Después de que Ana llegó uses a full clause rather than an infinitive. More advanced clauses may also require a mood choice.

mistakes.explanation: One o’clock uses singular la.
Keep de in antes de + infinitive.

practice.prompt: Say: at one o’clock.
practice.explanation: Use singular la with una.

practice.prompt: Say: on Mondays.
practice.explanation: The plural article indicates a recurring weekday.

practice.prompt: Complete: después de __. (eat)
practice.explanation: Use an infinitive directly after de.

takeaways: Use a la/a las with clock times.
Learn day and part-of-day phrases as patterns.
Antes de, después de and al can introduce infinitive actions.

indirect-objects.bigIdea: In a sentence about giving, offering or telling, the direct object is what is given or said. The indirect object identifies the recipient. Le and les point to recipients, not to the gender of a thing.
indirect-objects.goal: Identify recipients and choose me, te, le, nos or les.

build.title: Separate action, thing and recipient
build.body: Rosa le ofrece agua has Rosa as the subject, agua as the direct object and le as the person receiving the offer.

build.title: Choose the recipient pronoun
build.body: Me means to/for me, te to/for you informal, le to/for him/her/you formal, nos to/for us and les to/for them/you plural. Vosotros uses os in varieties that use that form.

build.title: Clarify the recipient with a phrase
build.body: Le doy agua a Ana is normal: le and a Ana refer to the same recipient. Les doy agua a los vecinos uses les because the recipients are plural.

extraExamples.explanation: Me identifies the listener receiving the story.
Te marks the recipient while un libro is the object brought.

items.spanish: Le doy un libro a Ana.
items.explanation: One recipient takes le.

items.spanish: Les doy un libro a Ana y Luis.
items.english: I give Ana and Luis a book.
items.explanation: Two recipients take les, even with one book.

closerLook.title: Le does not identify gender
closerLook.body: Le can refer to a male or female recipient or formal you. Context or a phrase such as a Rosa clarifies the identity.

closerLook.title: Recipients are a starting pattern
closerLook.body: Indirect objects also express experiencers, as in me gusta. Not every English for phrase is an indirect object, so learn the verb’s Spanish construction.

mistakes.explanation: Ana is the recipient here, represented by le.

mistakes.incorrect: Le doy agua a mis amigos.
mistakes.correct: Les doy agua a mis amigos.
mistakes.explanation: The recipient pronoun normally matches the plural recipients.

practice.prompt: In Rosa le ofrece agua, what is being offered?
practice.explanation: Water is the direct object; le identifies the recipient.

practice.prompt: Choose le or les for a Ana y Luis.
practice.explanation: There are two recipients.

practice.prompt: Say: Ana gives me a book.
practice.explanation: Me identifies the speaker as recipient.

takeaways: Distinguish the thing from the recipient.
Le/les reflect recipient number, not object gender.
A name or phrase can clarify the recipient.

pronoun-combinations.bigIdea: Spanish can replace both a recipient and a thing with pronouns. The recipient pronoun comes first, and le/les changes to se before lo, la, los or las.
pronoun-combinations.goal: Build combinations such as me lo and se la and place them with a verb.

build.title: Replace each role separately
build.body: Doy el libro a Ana can become Le doy el libro. Replacing el libro gives lo; combining the two roles requires a further change.

build.title: Use recipient before object
build.body: Me lo das means you give it to me. With le or les before lo/la/los/las, use se: Se lo doy. The se does not mean self here.

build.title: Place the group together
build.body: Se lo voy a dar and Voy a dárselo both work. Keep the pair together. Affirmative commands attach it: Dáselo; negative commands place it before: No se lo des.

extraExamples.english: I am going to give it to him/her/them/you formal.
extraExamples.explanation: Both pronouns attach to dar; the accent preserves the original stress.

extraExamples.english: Do not tell it to him/her/them/you formal.
extraExamples.explanation: The pair appears before a negative tú command.

contrast.title: The book changes; the recipient remains

items.explanation: Lo replaces el libro.
La replaces la llave; se still identifies the recipient indirectly.

closerLook.title: Se hides recipient number
closerLook.body: Se lo doy can have a singular or plural recipient. A Ana or a mis amigos makes the number and identity clear.

closerLook.title: Do not split the pair
closerLook.body: With a verb plus infinitive, choose a valid position for the whole group. Do not place one pronoun before the verb and another after the infinitive.

mistakes.explanation: Le changes to se before lo.
Recipient comes before direct-object pronoun.

practice.prompt: Replace both el libro and a Ana in Doy el libro a Ana.
practice.explanation: Le becomes se before lo.

practice.prompt: Choose: me las or las me.
practice.explanation: The recipient pronoun goes first.

practice.prompt: Give another position for Se lo voy a dar.
practice.explanation: Attach the complete group and preserve stress.

takeaways: Recipient comes before direct object.
Le/les becomes se before lo/la/los/las.
Keep the pronoun group together.

irregular-present.bigIdea: Knowing regular endings is necessary, but common verbs often change the stem too. Learn recurring patterns and the most frequent exceptions so familiar story verbs stop looking unrelated to their infinitives.
irregular-present.goal: Recognize common stem changes and irregular yo forms in the present.

build.title: Look for a stem-vowel change
build.body: Querer gives quiero/quieres but queremos. Poder gives puedo/puedes but podemos. Pedir gives pido/pides but pedimos. Many such verbs change outside nosotros and vosotros.

build.title: Notice special yo forms
build.body: Tener has tengo and venir has vengo. Their tú forms are tienes and vienes. Decir has digo and dices; these combine more than one change.

build.title: Learn frequent irregulars as small families
build.body: Ir has voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van; vosotros/vais is regional and not used in Sonora’s Latin American story model. Poner has pongo; hacer has hago; ver has veo. Do not infer the full paradigm from just one unusual form.

extraExamples.explanation: Nosotros pedimos keeps the stem vowel of pedir.
Pide shows the e-to-i change.

contrast.title: The subject changes the stem pattern

items.explanation: Poder changes o to ue in this form.
The nosotros form keeps o.

closerLook.title: Not a rule for every verb
closerLook.body: Comer keeps its stem in como; not every e or o changes. Learn the change with the verb rather than applying it to every similar spelling.

closerLook.title: Conjugated first verb, infinitive second
closerLook.body: Quiero volver and puedo leer still follow the infinitive pattern. Only the first verb carries the personal ending here.

mistakes.explanation: Tener has the irregular yo form tengo.
The common stem-change pattern does not change this nosotros stem.

practice.prompt: What infinitive gives quiere?
practice.explanation: The e changes to ie in this form.

practice.prompt: Complete: nosotros __ leer. (poder)
practice.explanation: Keep o for nosotros.

practice.prompt: Say: I have a key.
practice.explanation: Tener uses tengo for yo.

takeaways: Recognize stem changes as well as endings.
Check the nosotros form rather than spreading the change everywhere.
Learn the common irregular forms with their infinitives.

irregular-preterite.bigIdea: Many frequent past-tense verbs use a new stem or a special form. Readers need to recognize the family, not merely apply regular preterite endings.
irregular-preterite.goal: Read frequent irregular preterites and distinguish stem changes from spelling changes.

build.title: Learn the shared strong-stem endings
build.body: Tuve and other strong-stem preterites use -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron without the regular written accents. Tener → tuv-; estar → estuv-; poder → pud-; poner → pus-.

build.title: Recognize special families
build.body: Decir gives dije/dijo/dijeron, with -eron after j in the they form. Hacer gives hice/hizo/hicieron. Ser and ir share fui/fue/fueron; context distinguishes the meanings.

build.title: Separate spelling and sound changes
build.body: Buscar → busqué preserves the k sound. Leer → leyó changes the spelling in third person. Pedir → pidió and dormir → durmió change the stem vowel in third-person preterites.

extraExamples.explanation: Ver has short preterite forms such as vi and vio, written without accents.
Morir changes o to u in third-person preterite murió.

contrast.title: Regular and irregular past endings differ

items.explanation: A regular -ar third-person preterite ends in stressed -ó.
The strong-stem form tuvo has no written accent.

closerLook.title: Meaning comes from context
closerLook.body: Fue médica uses ser; fue a Madrid uses ir. The identical form alone cannot determine the infinitive.

closerLook.title: Recognition before memorizing every cell
closerLook.body: Start with fui/fue, dijo, tuvo, hizo, puso, pudo and vio in context. Then build each family’s other forms.

mistakes.explanation: Tener uses the strong preterite stem tuv-.
The j-stem family uses -eron, not -ieron, in this form.

practice.prompt: Which infinitive gives dijo?
practice.explanation: Dijo is a frequent irregular past form.

practice.prompt: Complete: ellos __ una idea. (tener)
practice.explanation: Use tuv- plus -ieron.

practice.prompt: Why is fue ambiguous without context?
practice.answer: It can come from ser or ir.
practice.explanation: The surrounding sentence distinguishes was from went.

takeaways: Learn common irregular stems as families.
Strong preterites differ from regular accented endings.
Use context to resolve shared forms.

demonstratives.bigIdea: Demonstratives point to something in physical space, time or the conversation. They can introduce a noun or stand in for one that the reader already understands.
demonstratives.goal: Match demonstratives to nouns and recover omitted nouns from context.

build.title: Choose a pointing family
build.body: Este/esta often presents something near the speaker; ese/esa something associated with the listener or already mentioned; aquel/aquella often something more distant. Context matters more than a fixed measurement.

build.title: Match gender and number
build.body: Este libro, esta llave, estos libros, estas llaves. Ese and aquel have matching sets: esos/esas and aquellos/aquellas.

build.title: Recover an understood noun
build.body: Esta llave abre la puerta; esa no. Esa stands for esa llave. La otra can likewise mean the other one when a feminine noun is understood.

extraExamples.explanation: La otra refers back to an understood feminine noun, such as semilla.
Aquel can place the hotel at a distance in space or in the remembered scene.

contrast.title: A noun can be expressed or understood

items.explanation: The noun llave is explicit.
Context supplies the omitted noun; esta remains feminine.

closerLook.title: Neutral pointing words
closerLook.body: Esto, eso and aquello can refer to an idea, event or unidentified thing. They do not introduce a noun: eso es extraño, not eso libro.

closerLook.title: Accent marks
closerLook.body: Modern standard spelling writes demonstratives such as este and esa without accents in ordinary use. Do not copy the tú/tu distinction onto demonstratives.

mistakes.explanation: Use the masculine noun modifier este before libro.
Match both gender and number.

practice.prompt: Say: these keys.
practice.explanation: Llaves is feminine plural.

practice.prompt: What noun is understood in La llave azul funciona; esa no?
practice.explanation: Esa refers to another key.

practice.prompt: Can eso directly introduce libro?
practice.explanation: Eso is a neutral standalone form.

takeaways: Use context to understand the pointing relationship.
Match noun gender and number.
An omitted noun can still determine the ending.

relative-clauses.bigIdea: A relative clause adds information about a person or thing. It contains a verb, but it belongs inside the larger sentence as a description. Finding the noun it describes prevents you from losing the main sentence.
relative-clauses.goal: Identify an antecedent and bracket its attached relative clause.

build.title: Find the noun being described
build.body: Una niña que sostenía una vela contains the noun niña followed by a clause describing her. Que points back to that noun.

build.title: Separate the main action from the description
build.body: Encontraron a una niña que sostenía una vela has encontraron as the main action. Sostenía is inside the description. Each verb can have a different subject or role.

build.title: Read other relative patterns
build.body: Donde can attach a location: el comedor, donde Rosa estaba colocando flores. Preposition + article + que appears in phrases such as la mesa sobre la que está el libro.

extraExamples.spanish: Entró al comedor, donde Rosa colocaba flores.
extraExamples.english: He/she entered the dining room, where Rosa was arranging flowers.
extraExamples.explanation: Donde attaches a location clause.

extraExamples.spanish: La mesa sobre la que está el libro es pequeña.
extraExamples.english: The table on which the book lies is small.
extraExamples.explanation: Sobre belongs with the relative phrase; the main description ends with es pequeña.

contrast.title: Que can play different roles inside the clause

items.spanish: La mujer que viene es Rosa.
items.english: The woman who is coming is Rosa.
items.explanation: Que represents the subject of viene.

items.spanish: La mujer que viste es Rosa.
items.english: The woman you saw is Rosa.
items.explanation: Que represents the object of viste; the implied subject is tú.

closerLook.title: Commas change the type of description
closerLook.body: Los vecinos que llegaron can identify a subset. Los vecinos, que llegaron tarde, adds extra information about the identified group. Do not ignore commas when interpreting reference.

closerLook.title: Known versus sought descriptions
closerLook.body: Conozco un libro que explica esto asserts that a book exists and describes it. Busco un libro que explique esto can describe a desired, not-yet-identified book. The mood choice needs context; the relative word que does not select a mood by itself.

mistakes.incorrect: El libro que lo compré. in a basic relative clause
mistakes.explanation: Do not normally repeat the same direct object with lo in this pattern.

mistakes.correct: Find its role in the clause
mistakes.explanation: Relative que points back to a noun; porque supplies a reason.

practice.prompt: Which noun does que describe in una niña que sostenía una vela?
practice.explanation: The attached clause describes the girl.

practice.prompt: Find the main verb in Leo el libro que compraste.
practice.explanation: Compraste is inside the relative description.

practice.prompt: Say: the book that I read.
practice.explanation: Que represents the book inside the clause.

takeaways: Find the noun the clause describes.
Separate the main verb from verbs inside descriptions.
Que may represent the subject or object of its clause.

content-clauses.bigIdea: In dice que…, que introduces what is said. Unlike relative que, it does not describe a preceding noun. The following clause has its own verb and may have its own subject.
content-clauses.goal: Distinguish content clauses, indirect questions and relative descriptions.

build.title: Find the reporting or thinking verb
build.body: Él dice que espera a alguien has dice as the main verb. Que espera a alguien supplies the content of his statement.

build.title: Track both subjects
build.body: Ana cree que Luis tiene la llave contains Ana as the thinker and Luis as the person who has the key. Do not carry the first subject automatically into the next clause.

build.title: Recognize embedded questions
build.body: Preguntó si alguien dormía asks whether someone was sleeping. No sabía dónde estaba expresses an indirect where question. Si here means whether, not a hypothetical if.

extraExamples.english: He/she asked whether anyone slept there.
extraExamples.explanation: Si introduces an indirect yes/no question.

extraExamples.spanish: No sé dónde está la llave.
extraExamples.english: I do not know where the key is.
extraExamples.explanation: Dónde retains its accent inside an indirect question.

items.english: He/she says that he/she has a book.
items.explanation: Que introduces the statement’s content.

items.english: He/she reads the book that he/she has.
items.explanation: Que introduces a description attached to libro.

closerLook.title: English can omit that
closerLook.body: English often says she thinks he is here. Spanish normally keeps que: Cree que está aquí.

closerLook.title: Mood depends on the governing expression
closerLook.body: Creo que viene normally uses indicative; no creo que venga normally uses subjunctive. Que by itself does not select a mood.

mistakes.explanation: Keep que to connect the statement content.

mistakes.incorrect: Assuming si always introduces a condition
mistakes.correct: Check the main verb and meaning
mistakes.explanation: Preguntó si… introduces a question about whether something is true.

practice.prompt: Identify the statement content in Dice que tiene tiempo.
practice.explanation: It tells us what is said.

practice.prompt: Does si mean a condition in Preguntó si venías?
practice.explanation: This is an embedded yes/no question.

practice.prompt: Complete: Creo __ Ana está aquí.
practice.explanation: Que links the belief to its content.

takeaways: Content clauses say what is said, thought or known.
Track subjects separately across clauses.
Indirect questions can use si or accented question words.

participles.bigIdea: A participle is a verb-derived form such as hablado, comido or escrito. It can help form a compound tense or describe a noun’s state. Those uses follow different agreement patterns.
participles.goal: Form common participles and decide whether agreement is required.

build.title: Build regular and common irregular forms
build.body: Regular -ar gives -ado; -er/-ir gives -ido. Common irregulars include hecho, dicho, visto, escrito, puesto, abierto, vuelto and muerto.

build.title: After haber, keep the participle fixed
build.body: He cerrado la puerta and he cerrado las puertas both use cerrado. The participle in this compound tense does not agree with the object.

build.title: As a description, match the noun
build.body: La puerta está cerrada and las puertas están cerradas use adjective-like agreement. Una advertencia escrita is feminine singular. Ser + participle can present a passive event: la puerta fue abierta por Ana.

extraExamples.explanation: Abiertas agrees with the feminine plural subject.

extraExamples.spanish: La puerta fue abierta por Ana.
extraExamples.english: The door was opened by Ana.
extraExamples.explanation: Ser + participle presents a passive event and the participle agrees with puerta.

items.explanation: Haber forms a tense; cerrado remains unchanged.
Estar presents a state; cerradas agrees with puertas.

closerLook.title: Not every adjective is a participle
closerLook.body: A description such as rojo is an adjective without being a verb’s participle. Ask whether there is a related verb and what construction the form belongs to.

closerLook.title: Result constructions
closerLook.body: La votación quedó aplazada presents the vote as left in a postponed state. Agreement works with votación; quedar adds a result meaning.

mistakes.explanation: After haber, do not agree the participle with the object.
A descriptive participle agrees with the noun.

practice.prompt: Give the participle of escribir.
practice.explanation: This is a common irregular participle.

practice.prompt: Complete: He __ las cartas. (escribir)
practice.explanation: Haber takes the fixed participle.

practice.prompt: Complete: Las cartas están __. (escribir)
practice.explanation: The description agrees with feminine plural cartas.

takeaways: Learn regular patterns and frequent irregular participles.
Haber + participle keeps the participle fixed.
Descriptive and passive participles agree with the noun.

present-perfect.bigIdea: The present perfect combines present haber with a participle. It often connects a past event with a present reference period, result or experience, but its frequency and contrast with the preterite vary by region.
present-perfect.goal: Recognize and form haber + participle without treating English tense choices as exact rules.

build.title: Conjugate haber
build.body: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han. This auxiliary is different from hay, the impersonal existence form.

build.title: Add the fixed participle
build.body: He leído means I have read. Hemos visto means we have seen. Keep the participle fixed, and put object pronouns before haber: lo he visto.

build.title: Read the present connection in context
build.body: Nunca he visto ese lugar expresses experience up to now. Some speakers prefer the perfect for today’s events; many Latin American varieties readily use the preterite instead.

extraExamples.explanation: Escrito stays fixed after ha.
Lo comes before the auxiliary, not between auxiliary and participle.

contrast.title: The reference point changes with haber

items.explanation: Present haber relates the event to now.
Imperfect haber places it before another past reference point.

closerLook.title: Regional usage matters
closerLook.body: Hoy fui and hoy he ido can both be natural, depending on variety and context. Do not label a Latin American preterite as wrong because an English translation uses have.

closerLook.title: Keep the verbal group together
closerLook.body: In the basic pattern, the auxiliary and participle form a unit. Place a short object pronoun before the auxiliary: lo he leído.

mistakes.incorrect: Tengo leído el libro. as a basic translation of I have read the book
mistakes.explanation: Use haber for this compound tense; tener constructions have different meanings and restrictions.
The participle remains fixed after haber.

practice.prompt: Say: we have eaten.
practice.explanation: Present haber + participle.

practice.prompt: Complete: Ana __ visto el mapa.
practice.explanation: Ha is the third-person singular auxiliary.

practice.prompt: Must every Spanish speaker use present perfect with hoy?
practice.explanation: Regional and contextual preferences vary.

takeaways: Present haber + participle relates an event to a present reference.
Keep the participle fixed and pronouns before the auxiliary.
Learn the regional contrast with the preterite.

pluperfect.bigIdea: A story can have more than one past layer. The pluperfect tells you something had already happened before the past moment currently being narrated.
pluperfect.goal: Recognize the earlier past and track its relationship to the story’s reference point.

build.title: Find the reference event
build.body: Cuando Daniel llegó, Rosa había preparado té has the arrival as a past reference point. Preparing tea happened earlier.

build.title: Build the compound
build.body: Use había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían plus a fixed participle: había viajado, habían salido.

build.title: Keep identity and order separate
build.body: Había can match yo, él, ella or usted. Context identifies the subject; the construction itself signals before a past reference, not a specific number of days earlier.

extraExamples.english: He/she had not seen the mark.
extraExamples.explanation: The lack of seeing is evaluated before a past reference point.

extraExamples.english: They had lived there for many years.
extraExamples.explanation: Habían matches a plural subject; vivido stays fixed.

items.explanation: Present reference.

items.english: Ana had gone out when I arrived.
items.explanation: Leaving is earlier than another past event.

closerLook.title: The reference can be implicit
closerLook.body: A previous sentence may establish the past moment. Not every pluperfect needs cuando in the same sentence.

closerLook.title: Negative and object pronouns
closerLook.body: No lo había visto keeps no and lo before había. Do not place lo between había and visto.

mistakes.explanation: The participle stays fixed after haber.

mistakes.incorrect: Assuming había viajado is simply another way to say viajó
mistakes.explanation: Pluperfect marks an earlier relationship; preterite presents the travel as an event in the narrative.

practice.prompt: What happened first in Llegué, pero Ana ya había salido?
practice.explanation: The pluperfect places leaving before the arrival.

practice.prompt: Say: they had eaten.
practice.explanation: Plural auxiliary plus fixed participle.

practice.prompt: Negate Lo había visto.
practice.explanation: No precedes the pronoun and auxiliary.

takeaways: Identify the past reference point.
Había + participle points earlier than that past.
The participle stays fixed.

progressive.bigIdea: A gerund such as leyendo or preparando can present an action as unfolding. Estar supplies the person and reference time; the gerund names the ongoing activity.
progressive.goal: Form common gerunds and interpret present and past progressive constructions.

build.title: Build the gerund
build.body: Regular -ar takes -ando; -er/-ir take -iendo. Leer gives leyendo; ir gives yendo; pedir gives pidiendo and dormir gives durmiendo.

build.title: Conjugate estar for the reference time
build.body: Estoy leyendo means I am reading now; estaba leyendo means I was reading at a past reference point. The gerund stays unchanged for different subjects.

build.title: Follow continuing activity
build.body: Seguir + gerund means continue/keep doing: seguía viendo el agua. A gerund can also describe an accompanying action, as in habló sonriendo.

extraExamples.english: He/she could still see the water.
extraExamples.explanation: Seguir + viendo presents continued seeing.
The gerund describes an accompanying action.

items.explanation: Simple present describes a routine here.
Estar + gerund foregrounds the unfolding action.

closerLook.title: English -ing has several Spanish equivalents
closerLook.body: Me gusta leer uses an infinitive, not a gerund. A Spanish gerund is not the default translation of every English -ing form.

closerLook.title: Pronoun placement
closerLook.body: Lo estoy leyendo and Estoy leyéndolo both work. Attaching lo requires an accent to preserve the gerund’s stress.

mistakes.explanation: An action liked is expressed with an infinitive here.
The gerund does not agree in number with the subject.

practice.prompt: Form the gerund of hablar.
practice.explanation: Replace -ar with -ando.

practice.prompt: Say: I was reading.
practice.explanation: Imperfect estar plus the gerund.

practice.prompt: Give another position for Lo estoy leyendo.
practice.explanation: Attach the pronoun and preserve stress.

takeaways: Estar supplies person and reference time.
The gerund stays unchanged.
Do not translate every English -ing form with a gerund.

verb-patterns.bigIdea: In multi-verb patterns, the first verb and its connecting word shape the meaning of the next action. Learn the complete frame, not just two verbs in isolation.
verb-patterns.goal: Decode frequent infinitive patterns found in the stories.

build.title: Start, stop or repeat
build.body: Empezar a + infinitive starts an action; dejar de stops it; volver a repeats it. The connecting preposition is part of the pattern.

build.title: Recognize recent completion
build.body: Acabar de + infinitive often expresses having just done something: acaba de llegar. In past narration, acababa de llegar means had just arrived.

build.title: Express necessity
build.body: Tener que + infinitive gives someone an obligation: tuvieron que elegir. Hay que + infinitive expresses a more general necessity without a named grammatical subject.

extraExamples.explanation: Acabar de locates a recent completion relative to the past scene.
Tener que expresses obligation, not possession.

contrast.title: A small connector changes the relationship

items.explanation: Volver a marks repetition.
Dejar de marks stopping.

closerLook.title: The first verb carries the person
closerLook.body: Puedo leer and podemos leer change the first verb while keeping leer. Modal patterns such as poder + infinitive need no connecting preposition.

closerLook.title: Pronouns depend on the construction
closerLook.body: Do not assume every two-verb combination permits every pronoun position. Learn common valid pairs such as lo voy a leer / voy a leerlo with the relevant construction.

mistakes.explanation: Empezar takes a in this pattern.
The action after tener que stays in the infinitive.

practice.prompt: What does dejó de funcionar tell you?
practice.explanation: Dejar de marks cessation.

practice.prompt: Say: she started reading.
practice.explanation: Use empezar a + infinitive.

practice.prompt: What does acababa de llegar add beyond llegó?
practice.answer: She/he had just arrived relative to the past scene.
practice.explanation: The construction expresses recent completion.

takeaways: Learn the first verb and connector together.
Keep the second action in the infinitive in these patterns.
Use the pattern to recognize start, stop, repetition, recent completion or obligation.

duration.bigIdea: Duration expressions depend on a reference moment. A situation may continue now, may have been continuing at a past moment, or may be a completed span. Similar English translations can hide these differences.
duration.goal: Use desde, hace and llevar to locate a situation in time.

build.title: Give a starting point or elapsed span
build.body: Vivo aquí desde 2020 gives a start date. Vivo aquí desde hace seis años gives elapsed time continuing now. Spanish commonly uses the present where English uses have lived.

build.title: Move the reference into the past
build.body: Vivía allí desde hacía ocho años describes eight years continuing up to a past reference point. The shift to vivía/hacía matters.

build.title: Distinguish a completed span or time ago
build.body: Vivió allí durante ocho años presents a completed span. Llegó hace ocho años locates arrival eight years before now. Lleva dos horas esperando expresses ongoing waiting; llevaba meses cerrada describes a state continuing at a past point.

extraExamples.explanation: Hace places a completed arrival before now.

extraExamples.english: The house had been closed for months.
extraExamples.explanation: Llevar plus a duration and state describes persistence up to the past scene.

items.spanish: Vivo aquí desde hace dos años.
items.english: I have lived here for two years.
items.explanation: The residence continues now.

items.english: I lived there for two years.
items.explanation: The residence is presented as a completed span.

closerLook.title: Llevar with an activity
closerLook.body: Llevo dos horas esperando combines a duration with a gerund. A state can instead be expressed by an agreeing adjective: lleva meses cerrada.

closerLook.title: Do not mechanically translate for as por
closerLook.body: Time expressions have their own constructions. Desde hace, durante and llevar organize time differently; choose the intended relationship first.

mistakes.correct: Vivo aquí desde hace dos años.
mistakes.explanation: Use hace with an elapsed quantity in this construction.

mistakes.incorrect: Measuring every hacía phrase from now
mistakes.explanation: Hacía measures the elapsed span from a past point.

practice.prompt: Say an ongoing two-year residence.
practice.answer: Vivo aquí desde hace dos años.
practice.explanation: Present vivo describes the situation continuing now.

practice.prompt: What does Llegó hace dos horas mean?
practice.explanation: Hace places the arrival before now.

practice.prompt: Why use hacía in Vivía allí desde hacía ocho años?
practice.answer: The reference point is in the past.
practice.explanation: The eight years extend up to that past point.

takeaways: Find the reference moment before translating the duration.
Desde + date and desde hace + quantity can describe ongoing situations.
Separate ongoing spans, completed spans and time ago.

reported-speech.bigIdea: Reported speech retells what someone said, thought or asked. The narrator’s viewpoint can change pronouns, tense and words such as today or here. Those changes follow meaning, not a blind replacement table.
reported-speech.goal: Read statements and questions reported from a past viewpoint.

build.title: Identify what is being reported
build.body: Dijo que tenía la llave reports the content of a statement. Le preguntó si tenía tiempo reports a yes/no question; si means whether.

build.title: Locate events relative to the report
build.body: A present situation in the original words can become imperfect in a past report: Tengo la llave → dijo que tenía la llave. An earlier completed event can be pluperfect: dijo que había salido.

build.title: Recalculate person, place and time
build.body: Voy mañana can become dijo que iría al día siguiente when the narrator reports later. Decide who I/you refers to and whether tomorrow still means the next day from now.

extraExamples.english: He/she asked whether anyone slept there.
extraExamples.explanation: An embedded yes/no question uses si.

extraExamples.spanish: Dijo que llegaría al día siguiente.
extraExamples.english: He/she said he/she would arrive the next day.
extraExamples.explanation: Conditional locates an arrival after the past statement; the time phrase follows that reference.

contrast.title: Direct words or a later report?

items.explanation: The quoted speaker uses her own present viewpoint.
The narrator reports from a past viewpoint.

closerLook.title: Backshift is not compulsory in every context
closerLook.body: Dijo que vive en Madrid can be natural if the speaker treats the residence as still current. Preserve the intended time relationship rather than changing every tense automatically.

closerLook.title: Reported questions keep their question word
closerLook.body: Preguntó dónde estaba retains dónde’s accent but does not require question marks when it is a statement reporting a question.

mistakes.incorrect: Dijo que yo tengo la llave. when the intended possessor is Ana
mistakes.correct: Ana dijo que tenía la llave.
mistakes.explanation: Resolve the original speaker before choosing the subject.

mistakes.incorrect: Assuming every si means hypothetical if
mistakes.explanation: After preguntar, si can mean whether.

practice.prompt: Report Ana dijo: «Tengo la llave» from a past viewpoint.
practice.answer: Ana dijo que tenía la llave.
practice.explanation: Tengo shifts to tenía in this past report.

practice.prompt: What does si introduce in Preguntó si venías?
practice.explanation: It is an indirect yes/no question.

practice.prompt: Which occurred earlier: explicó or había desaparecido?
practice.explanation: The pluperfect is earlier than the explanation.

takeaways: Find the reporting verb and its content.
Track person and time from the narrator’s viewpoint.
Backshift follows meaning and context, not a universal mechanical rule.

past-subjunctive.bigIdea: The imperfect subjunctive appears in past requests, wishes, evaluations and other subordinate constructions. It is not restricted to imaginary conditions, and its time value depends on the surrounding sentence.
past-subjunctive.goal: Form common -ra forms and relate them to a past governing verb.

build.title: Build from the preterite they form
build.body: Take hablaron, remove -ron, and add -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran: hablara, hablaras, hablara, habláramos, hablarais, hablaran. Tuvieron gives tuviera; dijeron gives dijera.

build.title: Read a past request or wish
build.body: Le pidió que explicara el sistema reports a request, not an assertion that the explanation happened. Esperó a que regresara la electricidad places the return inside an awaited event.

build.title: Relate the action to the main clause
build.body: Quería que vinieras can concern coming after the past desire. The name imperfect subjunctive does not mean every event is an ongoing past action like the indicative imperfect.

build.title: Recognize imagined comparisons
build.body: Como si estuvieran midiendo means as if they were measuring. Como si takes a past subjunctive form for the imagined comparison, even when a present observation provides the context: Me mira como si no me conociera.

extraExamples.explanation: Vinieras is the imperfect subjunctive of venir.

extraExamples.english: It was important that we arrive early.
extraExamples.explanation: The past evaluation takes llegáramos, with the nosotros accent.

contrast.title: Assert an event or request it?

items.english: He/she said he/she was explaining the system.
items.explanation: Indicative reports an asserted explanation.

items.english: He/she asked for the system to be explained.
items.explanation: Subjunctive presents the requested action.

closerLook.title: The -se series
closerLook.body: Hablase, tuviese and dijese are also standard imperfect subjunctive forms. Start with one series while learning to recognize both.

closerLook.title: Earlier than the past trigger
closerLook.body: Pidió que hubiera terminado antes… would use a compound subjunctive when an earlier completion is intended. Do not substitute a simple -ra form for every time relationship.

closerLook.title: An advanced concession in the B2 story
closerLook.body: Por convincente que le pareciera means however convincing it might seem to her. Por + adjective + que creates a concession; the subjunctive sets aside that degree of convincingness rather than asserting it as the reason for the next action.

mistakes.explanation: A past request normally takes a past subjunctive form here.
The nosotros form needs the accent on the correct syllable.

practice.prompt: Build tuviera from the preterite they form.
practice.explanation: Remove -ron and add -ra.

practice.prompt: Complete: Le pidió que __. (explicar)
practice.explanation: A past request governs the subjunctive here.

practice.prompt: Does vinieras always mean a completed event before the request?
practice.explanation: Its time relationship depends on the governing clause.

takeaways: Recognize -ra and -se as imperfect subjunctive series.
Past wishes and requests provide useful non-hypothetical contexts.
Use the governing clause to interpret the time relationship.

subjunctive-time.bigIdea: After expressions such as cuando and hasta que, an anticipated event can take subjunctive. A habitual or completed factual event usually takes indicative. The choice is about how the event is presented, not the connector alone.
subjunctive-time.goal: Compare factual and anticipated time clauses, including before and until.

build.title: Compare a habit with an awaited event
build.body: Cuando llega, llama describes a routine. Cuando llegue, llamará anticipates an arrival that has not happened at the reference point.

build.title: Read hasta que and antes de que
build.body: Esperaré hasta que vuelva anticipates the return. Antes de que venga uses subjunctive for the event the action precedes. With the same understood actor, antes de venir can use an infinitive instead.

build.title: Move the reference into the past
build.body: Esperó hasta que volviera presents a return awaited from a past point. Esperó hasta que volvió instead presents the return as an actual event that bounded the wait. Context determines the framing.

extraExamples.spanish: No vendas nada hasta que entiendas.
extraExamples.english: Do not sell anything until you understand.
extraExamples.explanation: Entiendas presents the understanding as awaited.

extraExamples.spanish: Salí antes de que llegara Ana.
extraExamples.explanation: Antes de que introduces the later arrival with subjunctive.

items.english: When he/she comes, he/she brings flowers.
items.explanation: A habitual visit uses indicative viene.

items.english: When he/she comes, he/she will bring flowers.
items.explanation: A future anticipated visit uses subjunctive venga.

closerLook.title: Avoid an English future inside the clause
closerLook.body: English when she comes also uses a present-looking form, but Spanish chooses subjunctive llegue/venga for an anticipated event in this pattern.

closerLook.title: Aunque needs its own meaning check
closerLook.body: Aunque + indicative can assert a fact; subjunctive can present information as hypothetical or set aside its factual status. It is not simply an always-uncertain switch.

mistakes.explanation: Use subjunctive for the anticipated event after cuando in this pattern.

mistakes.incorrect: Antes que Ana viene in this meaning
mistakes.explanation: Use the full connector and appropriate subjunctive.

practice.prompt: Complete a future plan: Cuando __, te llamaré. (llegar, yo)
practice.explanation: The arrival is anticipated.

practice.prompt: Complete a habit: Cuando __, llama. (llegar, él)
practice.explanation: The event is presented as habitual fact.

practice.prompt: Say before coming, with the same understood actor.
practice.explanation: An infinitive works when the actor is shared and understood.

takeaways: Distinguish habitual/completed facts from anticipated events.
Learn cuando, hasta que and antes de que with their meanings.
A past reference may call for past subjunctive.

prepositional-pronouns.bigIdea: Subject pronouns and pronouns after a preposition are not always the same. Para mí means for me; por ti means for you. This is a different position from me or te before a verb.
prepositional-pronouns.goal: Choose common prepositional pronouns and distinguish them from possessives and object pronouns.

build.title: Use mí and ti after common prepositions
build.body: Para mí, de mí and por ti use prepositional forms. Mí has an accent; ti does not. Él/ella/usted, nosotros/nosotras and ellos/ellas/ustedes keep familiar forms after these prepositions.

build.title: Learn conmigo and contigo
build.body: Con mí and con ti combine into conmigo and contigo. Con él and con ella remain separate. These special forms are not arbitrary spellings of me and te.

build.title: Check whether it is a pronoun or possessive
build.body: Para mí means for me. Mi casa means my house. Él is a pronoun; el libro uses the article. Position and meaning help distinguish them.

extraExamples.explanation: Conmigo is the combined form with me.
Ti has no written accent.

contrast.title: Owner or person after a preposition?

items.explanation: Mi modifies casa and has no accent.
Mí is a standalone pronoun after para and has an accent.

closerLook.title: Some prepositions use special patterns
closerLook.body: Entre tú y yo uses subject-like forms, not entre ti y mí. Do not extend the para mí pattern mechanically to every expression.

closerLook.title: Tonic and unstressed pronouns can appear together
closerLook.body: A mí me gusta emphasizes or clarifies the experiencer. Mí after a does not remove the need for me in this ordinary gustar pattern.

mistakes.explanation: Use the prepositional form mí here.
Con and ti combine into contigo.

practice.prompt: Say: for me.
practice.explanation: Use mí with an accent.

practice.prompt: Say: with you, addressing tú.
practice.explanation: Use the combined form.

practice.prompt: Does ti need an accent?
practice.explanation: Ti is written without one.

takeaways: Use mí and ti after common prepositions.
Learn conmigo and contigo as combined forms.
Distinguish mí from possessive mi.

narrative-connectors.bigIdea: Small linking words tell you how to connect one sentence to the next. They can mark a new stage, a continuing situation, an unexpected contrast or a correction to what you assumed.
narrative-connectors.goal: Use narrative markers to track sequence and expectations.

build.title: Follow sequence
build.body: Al principio, después, luego, al día siguiente and finalmente organize events. Mientras can place one action alongside another rather than simply after it.

build.title: Track continuation and change
build.body: Todavía follows something that continues; ya can indicate already or a new state. Ya no means no longer; todavía no means not yet.

build.title: Read contrast and concession
build.body: Sin embargo means however and links an unexpected contrast. Aunque introduces a concession: aunque llovía, salió. The mood in an aunque clause depends on how its content is presented.

extraExamples.explanation: Ya no marks the end of a previous situation.

extraExamples.english: It was raining; however, he/she went out.
extraExamples.explanation: Sin embargo sets up an unexpected contrast.

items.explanation: The arrival remains expected or relevant.
A former residence has ended.

closerLook.title: Mientras can link simultaneous events
closerLook.body: Mientras esperaba, leyó puts reading within the waiting period. Decide the time relationship before assigning tense roles.

closerLook.title: An explicit contrast helps comprehension
closerLook.body: No era una victoria definitiva, pero… limits a conclusion. A connector often tells you how strongly to interpret the preceding statement.

mistakes.incorrect: Reading ya no as not yet
mistakes.explanation: Todavía no expresses not yet.

mistakes.incorrect: Treating mientras as always meaning after
mistakes.explanation: Mientras usually frames overlapping time in this use.

practice.prompt: What does al día siguiente signal?
practice.answer: The following day relative to the story’s reference.
practice.explanation: It moves the narrative to a new time point.

practice.prompt: Translate todavía no.
practice.explanation: The event has not happened up to the reference point.

practice.prompt: What relationship does sin embargo signal?
practice.explanation: It asks you to connect the statements despite the tension.

pronominal-verbs.bigIdea: Not every verb with me, te or se describes an action literally done to oneself. Some verbs require these pronouns or change meaning with them. Learn the full verb pattern and its meaning in context.
pronominal-verbs.goal: Distinguish reflexive actions, lexical pronominal verbs and common changes of state.

build.title: Start with a literal reflexive contrast
build.body: Lava al niño describes washing someone else; se lava can describe washing himself/herself. This is one clear use, not the explanation for every se.

build.title: Learn the dictionary verb with se
build.body: Llamarse expresses having a name; arrepentirse expresses regret. Se llama Elena does not require imagining Elena literally calling herself.

build.title: Notice meaning and state changes
build.body: Irse often means leave; quedarse can mean stay or become left in a state; apagarse describes going out or switching off. Compare apagó la luz with la luz se apagó.

extraExamples.explanation: The lights undergo a change of state; they are not agents intentionally switching themselves off.
Quedarse contributes a resulting state in this context.

contrast.title: An agent causes it, or it happens to the subject

items.explanation: Ana causes the change; la luz is the object.
The light is the subject undergoing the change.

closerLook.title: Meaning depends on the verb
closerLook.body: Comer/comerse and ir/irse do not share one universal meaning difference. Check how the particular verb is used rather than assigning self to every pronoun.

closerLook.title: Other se constructions remain separate
closerLook.body: Se venden casas and se lo doy have different structures. The broader se lesson helps distinguish passive-like, impersonal and pronoun-replacement uses.

mistakes.incorrect: Translating every se as himself or herself
mistakes.explanation: Se llama and se apagó need a construction-specific meaning.
The pronoun still follows the subject in the naming pattern.

practice.prompt: What does Se llama Elena mean?
practice.explanation: Treat llamarse as a naming construction.

practice.prompt: Who is the subject in La luz se apagó?
practice.explanation: The light undergoes the change.

practice.prompt: Say: my name is Ana.

takeaways: Reflexive is one use of the pronouns, not a universal translation.
Learn pronominal verbs as complete entries.
Track whether the subject causes or undergoes a change.

quantifiers.bigIdea: Words such as cada, otro and alguno organize groups of things or people. They can introduce nouns, stand for understood nouns, or express the absence of something.
quantifiers.goal: Read common quantifiers and recognize noun omission in story references.

build.title: Distinguish each from all
build.body: Cada jueves means every Thursday and keeps jueves singular. Todos los jueves refers to all Thursdays in the repeated set. Todo/toda/todos/todas agree with the noun.

build.title: Read another and some
build.body: Otra nota means another note without adding una before otra. Algún libro and ningún libro use shortened forms before masculine singular nouns; algunas cartas and ninguna carta follow gender and number.

build.title: Recover what is understood
build.body: Unas semillas… la otra refers to another seed. La más alta can refer to the tallest line after líneas has been established. Lo que instead can mean what/the thing that without a named noun.

extraExamples.spanish: Algunos vecinos ya no vivían allí.
extraExamples.english: Some neighbors no longer lived there.
extraExamples.explanation: Algunos matches masculine plural vecinos.

extraExamples.spanish: La más alta alcanzaba el techo.
extraExamples.english: The highest one reached the ceiling.
extraExamples.explanation: A feminine noun such as línea is understood from context.

contrast.title: A noun is named or recovered

items.explanation: The noun is expressed.
Context supplies semilla; feminine agreement remains.

closerLook.title: People and things can have different negative words
closerLook.body: Nadie refers to nobody; nada to nothing. Ningún libro modifies a noun. These are related meanings with different grammatical uses.

closerLook.title: Neutral lo does not always replace a masculine object
closerLook.body: Lo que no explicaba means what it did not explain. Lo poco que queda means the little that remains. These package information or a degree rather than pointing to a masculine noun.

mistakes.explanation: Do not add una before otra in the basic another pattern.
Cada normally takes a singular count unit; jueves already has the same singular/plural spelling.
